Portainer plugin management API access (CVE-2026-44848) AIExploitation High
Hunts HTTP POST requests to Portainer's /docker/plugins/pull and /docker/plugins/{name}/enable proxy endpoints, which bypass Portainer-side RBAC in vulnerable releases (<2.33.8, <2.39.2, <2.41.0) because /plugins is absent from prefixProxyFuncMap and falls through to executeDockerRequest unauthorized. Rationale: Article identifies the exact vulnerable endpoints (POST /plugins/pull, POST /plugins/{name}/enable) and shows in the Go source excerpt that /plugins is NOT in prefixProxyFuncMap so it bypasses Portainer's authorization wrapper. A successful POST against this URI from a non-admin session is unambiguous exploitation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rrmm-9v76-h3p4
ATT&CKT1190 T1068
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portainer administrator legitimately installing a Docker volume/log/network plugin from a trusted registry
  • Automation tooling (Ansible/Terraform) using a Portainer admin token to provision plugins after a node rebuild
  • Internal CI/CD pipeline calling the plugin API with a service account during cluster bootstrap
  • Pentest or red-team exercise validating this advisory
  • GET requests from health-check scrapers (excluded by the POST predicate)
Suppression filter
| where csUserName !in~ ("portainer-admin","ansible-portainer","terraform-portainer")
Response runbook
1. Triage: Open the matched proxy/IIS log line and extract csUserName / Portainer JWT subject and source IP; confirm whether that identity holds the Portainer admin role. 2. Contain: Disable the user in Portainer or revoke its Docker-endpoint access, isolate the target Docker host, and quarantine any plugin under /var/lib/docker/plugins/ created within +/- 10 minutes of the request. 3. Hunt: Pivot to host telemetry (UC2/UC3) on the same DeviceName / timestamp window, look for chroot or nsenter from the plugin container, and audit /etc/docker/plugins for new manifests. Upgrade Portainer to 2.33.8 / 2.39.2 / 2.41.0+.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod =~ "POST"
| where csUriStem matches regex @"(?i)/api/endpoints/\d+/docker/plugins/(pull|.+/enable)"
| where scStatus < 400
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csUserName, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, scStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Docker plugin runtime spawned from /var/lib/docker/plugins/ on host (CVE-2026-44848) AIInstallation High
Hunts Linux process executions whose binary path begins with /var/lib/docker/plugins/<digest>/rootfs/ and whose parent is dockerd/containerd/runc. Any post-exploit plugin pushed through the unauthorized /plugins/pull + /plugins/{name}/enable chain lands here and executes as root with whatever capabilities (CAP_SYS_ADMIN, host bind mounts) the plugin manifest requested. Rationale: Article states 'Docker plugins execute as root on the host' and the Linux runtime path for an enabled plugin is /var/lib/docker/plugins/<digest>/rootfs/. Pairing that image-path prefix with a containerd/dockerd parent yields a near-zero-FP signal because plugin install is normally an admin-only, low-frequency event. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rrmm-9v76-h3p4 • https://docs.docker.com/engine/extend/plugin_api/
ATT&CKT1068 T1611 T1610
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Administrator legitimately installing a known Docker volume plugin (rexray, vieux/sshfs)
  • CI/CD pipeline reinstalling a vetted log driver plugin after a node rebuild
  • Kubernetes CSI plugin operator installing a storage driver
  • Backup software (Velero/Restic) shipping a Docker volume plugin
  • Docker engine upgrade re-creating plugin rootfs paths
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("rexray","vieux/sshfs","docker/telemetry","weaveworks/net-plugin")
Response runbook
1. Triage: Read /var/lib/docker/plugins/<digest>/config.json and inspect for CAP_SYS_ADMIN, propagatedMount, host-path bind mounts, or an untrusted registry origin; correlate with UC1 W3CIISLog/proxy events on the same host+time to identify the Portainer user. 2. Contain: `docker plugin disable <name>` then `docker plugin rm -f <name>`, isolate the host from the network, snapshot for forensics, and rotate any credentials reachable from the host. 3. Hunt: Search the cluster for the same plugin digest, audit other Portainer endpoints accessed by that user, and review auth.log + bash history for chroot/nsenter/mount activity originating from the plugin container.

Docker daemon plugin install/enable event from non-admin context (CVE-2026-44848) AIInstallation Medium
Surfaces dockerd syslog entries recording plugin pull/install/enable operations. Combined with UC1 (HTTP) and UC2 (process), this is the daemon-side proof of plugin registration and remains useful on hosts that do not run EDR but ship dockerd journald/syslog to the SIEM. Rationale: Article's affected-code excerpt shows requests fall through to executeDockerRequest and are forwarded to dockerd, so the dockerd log is the daemon-side fingerprint of /plugins/pull and /plugins/{name}/enable activity. This UC corroborates UC1+UC2 on hosts without EDR. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rrmm-9v76-h3p4
ATT&CKT1610 T1068
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin operator running `docker plugin install` from the CLI for a vetted plugin
  • Docker engine restart replaying plugin-enable events from /var/lib/docker/plugins
  • Swarm rebuild rolling plugins back onto fresh nodes
  • Kubernetes node lifecycle reinstalling logging/storage drivers
  • Plugin upgrade as part of routine patching
Suppression filter
| where PluginName !in~ ("rexray","vieux/sshfs","weaveworks/net-plugin","docker/telemetry")
Response runbook
1. Triage: Extract the plugin name + digest from the dockerd line, list current plugins (`docker plugin ls --no-trunc`), and inspect the manifest for excessive privileges or an unknown registry. 2. Contain: Disable and remove the plugin (`docker plugin disable <name>` then `docker plugin rm -f <name>`), then rotate any credentials accessible from the host. 3. Hunt: Pivot to UC1 (proxy/IIS) by host+timestamp to find which Portainer user triggered the install, and to UC2 to enumerate binaries that ran from /var/lib/docker/plugins.

| order by TimeGenerated desc

n8n host inventory hunt — surface vulnerable instances < 1.123.43 / 2.20.7 / 2.22.1 AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunt for hosts running n8n (Node.js parent process or n8n-nodes-base in cmdline) so SOC can cross-reference patched-version state against CVE-2026-44791. This is asset-surface enumeration for the n8n RCE patch bypass — runs read-only and identifies hosts to escalate to vulnerability management. Rationale: Article explicitly names affected packages npm:n8n with version ranges <1.123.43 / 2.20.7 / 2.22.1 and lists NODES_EXCLUDE=n8n-nodes-base.xml as the only workaround. The 'n8n' string in node.exe cmdline is the canonical fingerprint of an n8n instance running on a host — no Defender TVM signature exists for npm packages so process-telemetry is the only practical asset hunt. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/security/advisories/GHSA-hqr4-h3xv-9m3r • https://cybersecuritynews.com/n8n-rce-vulnerabilities/ • https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/security
ATT&CKT1190

  • CI/CD runners that pull n8n containers for integration tests
  • DevOps engineer running `n8n start` interactively to demo a workflow
  • Internal staging n8n deployments behind VPN (in scope for patching but lower urgency)
  • Documentation builds that render n8n docs and reference the binary in path

Triage — for each surfaced host, capture full process tree and check whether the n8n version on disk falls inside <1.123.43, ≥2.21.0 & <2.22.1, or ≥2.0.0-rc.0 & <2.20.7 ranges (run `n8n --version` or inspect package.json). 2. Contain — for production n8n hosts not yet on a patched release, immediately apply the NODES_EXCLUDE=n8n-nodes-base.xml workaround and restrict workflow create/edit permissions to admin only; schedule emergency upgrade. 3. Hunt — pivot to UC2 to look for any post-exploit shell-spawn evidence on each vulnerable host going back the host's full retention; review n8n credential store for unexpected webhook URLs or executable workflow nodes added since vulnerable version was deployed.

n8n Node.js parent spawning OS shell — post-exploit RCE indicator for CVE-2026-44791 AIExploitation High
Detects the realised RCE outcome of the XML-node prototype-pollution patch bypass: an n8n Node.js process (commandline references n8n / n8n-nodes-base) spawning cmd/powershell/sh/bash with download, base64, reverse-shell, or temp-directory cmdline hallmarks. Article states 'when combined with other nodes, this could lead to RCE on the n8n host' — this catches that exact host-side execution shape. Rationale: Article: 'When combined with other nodes, this could lead to RCE on the n8n host.' n8n runs as a Node.js process; the prototype-pollution → RCE chain manifests as the Node parent spawning an OS shell with attacker-controlled cmdline. Parent fingerprint = node + n8n in cmdline (high-precision asset filter). Child = shell binary. Cmdline tokens = the standard reverse-shell / download cradle vocabulary from public n8n CVE-2026-44789/44790/44791 trio writeups (cross-checked against the CyberSecurityNews coverage that catalogs the trio). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/security/advisories/GHSA-hqr4-h3xv-9m3r • https://cybersecuritynews.com/n8n-rce-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.001 T1059.004 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate workflow using n8n's built-in 'Execute Command' node to run `curl https://api.example.com/...` against an approved API
  • n8n container post-deploy startup script invoking `bash -c 'wait-for-it db:5432'`
  • SRE debugging an n8n pod with `kubectl exec -- bash` (parent will be node, child bash, but cmdline is interactive)
  • Backup workflow that pipes data through `base64` for safe transport in a JSON field
  • Workflow that uses `wget` to fetch a CSV from an internal data lake on /tmp scratch
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("wait-for-it","healthcheck","livenessProbe","readinessProbe") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("wait-for-it","--health-cmd","livenessProbe","readinessProbe"))
| where not (ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)curl\s+(-fsSL\s+)?https?://[^ ]*(\.corp\.|\.internal\.|localhost|127\.0\.0\.1)")
Response runbook
1. Triage — pull the exact n8n workflow that triggered the shell spawn (correlate timestamp to n8n execution log on the host; n8n logs workflowId per run) and verify the workflow legitimately contains an Execute Command node performing this action; if no matching workflow exists, treat as confirmed exploitation. 2. Contain — isolate the n8n host from the network, kill node process and any spawned shells, rotate every credential stored in n8n's credential store (DB creds, API keys, webhook secrets), and revoke any active webhook URLs. 3. Hunt — search 30 days back for outbound network connections from node parent process to non-corporate IPs (suspect C2), file writes to /tmp /var/tmp /dev/shm by node, new cron jobs / systemd units / Run-key entries, and any workflow modifications by non-admin n8n users; pivot to other n8n hosts in scope (UC1 inventory) for the same TTP.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("n8n","n8n-nodes-base")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl ","wget ","Invoke-WebRequest","IEX","Invoke-Expression","base64 ","-EncodedCommand","/tmp/","%TEMP%","bash -i","nc -e","perl -e","python -c")
   or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)/dev/tcp/"
   or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bnc\b.*\b-l\b"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let Lookback = 7d;
let ShellChildren = dynamic(["cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh"]);
let SusTokens = dynamic(["curl ","wget ","Invoke-WebRequest","IEX","Invoke-Expression","base64 ","-EncodedCommand","/tmp/","%TEMP%","bash -i","nc -e","perl -e","python -c"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
  | where EventID == 4688
  | where ParentProcessName has "\\node.exe"
  | extend ChildBin = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName,"\\")[-1]))
  | where ChildBin in (ShellChildren)
  | where CommandLine has_any (SusTokens) or CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)/dev/tcp/"
  | where TargetUserName !endswith "$"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = TargetUserName,
            ParentCmd = ParentProcessName, ChildImage = NewProcessName, ChildCmd = CommandLine),
(ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
  | where ParentProcessName has "node"
  | where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("n8n","n8n-nodes-base")
  | extend ChildBin = tolower(tostring(split(ActingProcessName,"/")[-1]))
  | where ChildBin in (ShellChildren)
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (SusTokens) or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)/dev/tcp/"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, Account = ActorUsername,
            ParentCmd = ParentProcessCommandLine, ChildImage = ActingProcessName, ChildCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).

n8n workflow API request body containing JS prototype pollution tokens (CVE-2026-44789) AIExploitation High
Hunts for HTTP requests to the n8n workflow/execution API whose body or query string contains JavaScript prototype-pollution sentinels (`__proto__`, `constructor.prototype`, `__defineGetter__`) targeting the HTTP Request node pagination parameter. This is the article-specific pre-exploit signal for CVE-2026-44789. Rationale: Pivots on the exact prototype-pollution sentinels (`__proto__`, `constructor.prototype`, `__defineGetter__`) named in CWE-1321 / GHSA-c8xv-5998-g76h, scoped to the n8n REST/webhook URL surface where the pagination parameter is parsed. Cross-checked against GitHub GHSA advisory, Endor Labs write-up, and Cybersecurity News reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c8xv-5998-g76h • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-44789 • https://www.endorlabs.com/learn/ • https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1321.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal AppSec / DAST scanners (Burp Suite, Acunetix, Nessus, Nuclei) running prototype-pollution test payloads against n8n instances in dev/staging
  • Legitimate workflow authors saving a workflow whose JSON body literally contains the string `__proto__` (rare but possible in JS-tutorial workflows)
  • Bug-bounty researchers probing public-facing n8n with permission, generating identical telemetry
  • Penetration tests of the n8n perimeter where the same payload list is reused
  • URL-encoded user input in unrelated webhook calls where `%5F` characters happen to align
Suppression filter
| where ClientIP !in ("<scanner-vlan-cidr>") and UA !has_any ("Burp", "Nessus", "Nuclei", "Acunetix", "sqlmap", "ZAP")
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): pull the full HTTP request body and source IP. Confirm whether the URL hits `/rest/workflows`, `/rest/executions`, or `/webhook`; check `User-Agent` and `csUserName` for known scanner signatures or authenticated user identity. Pull n8n version from the host (`npm ls n8n` or container image tag) — confirm version is in vulnerable range (<1.123.43, 2.x <2.20.7, 2.21+ <2.22.1). Step 2 (Contain): if source IP is external and unauthenticated, block at WAF/reverse proxy. If authenticated, force-revoke the user's API tokens, suspend account, and snapshot the n8n DB for forensics. Disable the HTTP Request node via `NODES_EXCLUDE=n8n-nodes-base.httpRequest` until upgrade lands. Step 3 (Hunt): pivot on the n8n host AID — look for `node.exe`/`node` spawning `cmd.exe`, `sh`, `powershell.exe`, or LOLBins in the following 60 minutes; check `AsepValueUpdate` / cron for persistence; review egress to non-org IPs from the n8n host.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let PollutionTokens = dynamic(["__proto__", "constructor.prototype", "__defineGetter__", "prototype[", "%5F%5Fproto%5F%5F", "%5Fproto%5F"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where RemotePort in (5678, 443, 80) or LocalPort in (5678, 443, 80)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("node.exe", "n8n.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "n8n"
| where RemoteUrl has_any (PollutionTokens)
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (PollutionTokens)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, LocalPort, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let PollutionTokens = dynamic(["__proto__", "constructor.prototype", "__defineGetter__", "prototype[", "%5F%5Fproto%5F%5F", "%5Fproto%5F"]);
let IISHits = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where csUriStem has_any ("/rest/workflows", "/rest/executions", "/webhook")
    | where csUriQuery has_any (PollutionTokens) or csUriStem has_any (PollutionTokens)
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = Computer, ClientIP = cIP, User = csUserName,
              Method = csMethod, Uri = csUriStem, Query = csUriQuery, UA = csUserAgent,
              Source = "W3CIISLog";
let CSLHits = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where RequestURL has_any ("/rest/workflows", "/rest/executions", "/webhook")
    | where RequestURL has_any (PollutionTokens) or Message has_any (PollutionTokens)
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = DestinationHostName, ClientIP = SourceIP,
              User = SourceUserName, Method = RequestMethod, Uri = RequestURL,
              Query = RequestContext, UA = RequestClientApplication,
              Source = "CommonSecurityLog";
let WebHits = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where Url has_any ("/rest/workflows", "/rest/executions", "/webhook")
    | where Url has_any (PollutionTokens) or UrlOriginal has_any (PollutionTokens)
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = DvcHostname, ClientIP = SrcIpAddr,
              User = SrcUsername, Method = HttpMethod, Uri = Url,
              Query = UrlOriginal, UA = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent,
              Source = "ImWebSession";
union isfuzzy=true IISHits, CSLHits, WebHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: n8n HTTP Request Node Pagination Prototype Pollution Tokens (CVE-2026-44789)
id: 7e3b2a4c-1f5d-4e9a-8c7f-2d6b3a1c4e8f
description: Detects HTTP requests to n8n workflow/execution/webhook API endpoints whose URI or query string carries JavaScript prototype-pollution sentinel tokens used to exploit CVE-2026-44789 in the HTTP Request node pagination handler.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c8xv-5998-g76h
  - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-44789
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/20
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.007
  - cve.2026.44789
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_uri:
    cs-uri-stem|contains:
      - '/rest/workflows'
      - '/rest/executions'
      - '/webhook'
  selection_payload:
    cs-uri-query|contains:
      - '__proto__'
      - 'constructor.prototype'
      - '__defineGetter__'
      - 'prototype['
      - '%5F%5Fproto%5F%5F'
  condition: selection_uri and selection_payload
falsepositives:
  - JavaScript prototype-pollution scanners (Burp, Acunetix, Nessus) run by internal security teams
  - Legitimate developer use of `__proto__` as a literal string in a workflow body (rare)
level: high
(source:windows.sysmon OR source:nginx OR source:apache OR source:aws.alb OR source:cloudflare) (@http.url:(*"/rest/workflows"* OR *"/rest/executions"* OR *"/webhook"*) OR @url:(*"/rest/workflows"* OR *"/rest/executions"* OR *"/webhook"*)) (@http.url:(*__proto__* OR *constructor.prototype* OR *__defineGetter__* OR *%5F%5Fproto%5F%5F*) OR @url:(*__proto__* OR *constructor.prototype* OR *__defineGetter__*) OR @http.url_details.queryString:(*__proto__* OR *constructor.prototype*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/node(\.exe)?$/i
| (regex("--inspect", field=CommandLine) OR regex("n8n", field=CommandLine))
| (regex("__proto__", field=CommandLine) OR regex("constructor\.prototype", field=CommandLine) OR regex("__defineGetter__", field=CommandLine))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
WEB

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.url) as url values(Web.http_method) as http_method values(Web.src) as src from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/rest/workflows*" OR Web.url="*/rest/executions*" OR Web.url="*/webhook*" by Web.dest Web.user Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | search url="*__proto__*" OR url="*constructor.prototype*" OR url="*__defineGetter__*" OR url="*prototype%5B*" | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Post-exploit RCE: node.js (n8n) spawning shell or scripting interpreter AIInstallation High
Detects the post-exploitation tail of CVE-2026-44789 — the n8n `node` process spawning a shell (`cmd.exe`, `sh`, `bash`, `powershell.exe`) or a LOLBin. Prototype-pollution RCEs land here because the polluted global lets the attacker reroute child-process spawning into arbitrary commands run as the n8n service account. Rationale: Uses the most reliable post-exploit signal — n8n's `node` process spawning a shell or LOLBin — which is the actual outcome chain described in GHSA-c8xv-5998-g76h ("combined with other techniques this could lead to RCE"). Article + Endor Labs corroboration both flag RCE as the impact, and CWE-1321 prototype-pollution chains universally land via hijacked child-process spawn. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c8xv-5998-g76h • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-44789 • https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1321.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/
ATT&CKT1059 T1059.001 T1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate use of the n8n Execute Command node (`n8n-nodes-base.executeCommand`) by an authorised workflow — verify the workflow owner and content
  • n8n custom community nodes that legitimately invoke `curl`/`wget` for file fetching
  • Node-based CI/CD agents running on the same host that spawn shells for build tasks
  • Diagnostic / troubleshooting scripts where an admin manually exec'd into the n8n container and ran `sh`
  • Docker entrypoint chains where the n8n container's `node` PID 1 spawns `sh -c` for shutdown handling
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "n8n-nodes-base.executeCommand") and not (DeviceName has_any ("build-", "ci-", "jenkins-")) and not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "docker-entrypoint")
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): pull the parent `node` command line and the child cmd line — confirm the parent is n8n (check folder path for `/n8n/`, `.n8n`, or `n8n-nodes-base`). Pull the n8n version via `npm ls n8n` or container image tag; confirm vulnerable range. Check whether the workflow that spawned the shell is documented to use the Execute Command node. Step 2 (Contain): isolate the n8n host via Defender / Falcon Real-Time Response. Kill the child process tree. Rotate the n8n encryption key (`N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY`) and DB credentials. If the host is internet-facing, take it off the load balancer. Step 3 (Hunt): retrospectively search the n8n web logs over the previous 30 days for the prototype-pollution URI patterns from UC1; inventory all workflows for unexpected Execute Command nodes; correlate against `AsepValueUpdate` for new persistence and outbound `DnsRequest` / `NetworkConnectIP4` from the n8n host to non-org infrastructure.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let ShellsAndLolbins = dynamic(["cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","zsh","dash","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","nc","ncat","socat"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("n8n", "\\n8n\\", "/n8n/")
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("n8n", "\\.n8n\\")
| where FileName in~ (ShellsAndLolbins)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AccountDomain,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let ShellsAndLolbins = dynamic(["cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","zsh","dash","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","nc","ncat","socat"]);
let WinHits = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","node\\","\\node")
    | where tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]) in~ (ShellsAndLolbins)
    | where (CommandLine has_any ("n8n")) or (ParentProcessName has "n8n") or true
    | where TargetUserName !endswith "$"
    | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, User=TargetUserName,
              ParentImage=ParentProcessName, ChildImage=NewProcessName,
              ChildCmd=CommandLine, Source="SecurityEvent";
let AsimHits = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","node")
    | where ActingProcessName has_any (ShellsAndLolbins) or TargetProcessName has_any (ShellsAndLolbins)
    | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
    | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, User=ActorUsername,
              ParentImage=ParentProcessName, ChildImage=coalesce(TargetProcessName, ActingProcessName),
              ChildCmd=coalesce(TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine),
              Source="ImProcessCreate";
union isfuzzy=true WinHits, AsimHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: n8n node.js Process Spawning Shell or LOLBin (CVE-2026-44789 Post-Exploit)
id: 4a8f1e6c-9d3b-4c7a-b2e5-f8a1c4d6e9b3
description: Detects post-exploitation of CVE-2026-44789 in n8n where the node.js process hosting n8n spawns a shell or living-off-the-land binary. The pagination prototype-pollution chain hijacks child-process invocation to launch attacker-controlled commands as the n8n service account.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c8xv-5998-g76h
  - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-44789

detection:

      - '\node.exe'

  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'

      - '/bash'
      - '/zsh'
      - '/dash'

      - '\certutil.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'

falsepositives:

  - Build pipelines where node spawns shells for compilation tasks
level: high
(source:windows.security OR source:windows.sysmon OR source:linux.auditd) (@ParentImage:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe OR */node) OR @process.parent.executable.path:(*\\node.exe OR */node)) (@Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\rundll32.exe OR *\\regsvr32.exe OR *\\certutil.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\wget.exe) OR @process.executable.path:(*/sh OR */bash OR */zsh OR */dash OR */nc OR */ncat OR */socat OR */curl OR */wget)) -@User:*$
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/^node(\.exe)?$/i
| ImageFileName=/(cmd|powershell|pwsh|sh|bash|zsh|dash|mshta|wscript|cscript|rundll32|regsvr32|certutil|bitsadmin|curl|wget|nc|ncat|socat)(\.exe)?$/i
| NOT regex("\\$$", field=UserName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
| _count > 0

Vulnerable n8n versions in TVM inventory (CVE-2026-44789) AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces hosts and software packages where n8n is installed at a version inside the CVE-2026-44789 vulnerable range (<1.123.43, 2.0.0-rc.0–2.20.6, 2.21.0–2.22.0). Pre-exploit asset visibility — without this UC the SOC is hunting blind for an attack surface they don't know they own. Rationale: Article explicitly enumerates vulnerable version ranges (npm:n8n <1.123.43; 2.0.0-rc.0–<2.20.7; 2.21.0–<2.22.1) — version-range matching against TVM inventory is the lowest-FP detection possible and the most operationally valuable pre-attack signal. Corroborated against the NVD CVE entry and the published patched versions. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c8xv-5998-g76h • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-44789
ATT&CKT1592.002 T1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM inventory reporting a vulnerable version on a host where n8n has already been uninstalled but software inventory hasn't refreshed
  • n8n running inside a container that's flagged as 'host' for software inventory — the running image version is fine, but the host's static n8n install isn't
  • Development/sandbox hosts running deliberately vulnerable versions for security research (should be on an allow-list)
  • Sub-component of another product (e.g. embedded SDK) carrying an `n8n` substring but not the actual n8n product
  • Host has been patched but Defender TVM has not yet re-scanned and reflected the new version
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox-", "research-", "dvwa-")) and SoftwareName =~ "n8n"
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): for each hit, cross-check the device's `IsInternetFacing` flag and the n8n exposure path (LB / reverse proxy / direct). Hosts with `IsInternetFacing == true` are P1; internal-only hosts are P2. Pull workflow inventory and user list if accessible. Step 2 (Contain): apply the n8n-published patched version (1.123.43, 2.20.7, or 2.22.1) via your patch-management pipeline; for hosts you can't upgrade immediately, set `NODES_EXCLUDE=n8n-nodes-base.httpRequest` and restrict workflow-edit RBAC to a small admin group. Step 3 (Hunt): retrospectively run UC1 (URL-token hunt) over the last 30 days against each vulnerable host's web logs to detect any prior exploitation; pair with UC2 (post-RCE shell-spawn hunt) over the same window.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName =~ "n8n" or SoftwareName has "n8n"
| extend Parts = split(SoftwareVersion, ".")
| extend Major = toint(Parts[0]), Minor = toint(Parts[1]), Patch = toint(Parts[2])
| extend Vulnerable = case(
    Major == 1 and (Minor < 123 or (Minor == 123 and Patch < 43)), "yes-1.x (<1.123.43)",
    Major == 2 and Minor >= 0 and Minor <= 19, strcat("yes-2.", tostring(Minor), " (<2.20.7)"),
    Major == 2 and Minor == 20 and Patch < 7, "yes-2.20.<7",
    Major == 2 and Minor == 21, "yes-2.21 (<2.22.1)",
    Major == 2 and Minor == 22 and Patch < 1, "yes-2.22.0",
    "no")
| where Vulnerable != "no"
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId | project DeviceId, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, Vulnerable, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where CveId =~ "CVE-2026-44789" or SoftwareName has "n8n"
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceId, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceId | project DeviceId, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform) on DeviceId
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion,
          CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc
(source:cspm OR source:tenable OR source:qualys OR source:rapid7) (@vulnerability.cve:CVE-2026-44789 OR (@software.name:n8n AND @software.version:(1.* OR 2.0.* OR 2.1.* OR 2.2.* OR 2.3.* OR 2.4.* OR 2.5.* OR 2.6.* OR 2.7.* OR 2.8.* OR 2.9.* OR 2.10.* OR 2.11.* OR 2.12.* OR 2.13.* OR 2.14.* OR 2.15.* OR 2.16.* OR 2.17.* OR 2.18.* OR 2.19.* OR 2.20.0 OR 2.20.1 OR 2.20.2 OR 2.20.3 OR 2.20.4 OR 2.20.5 OR 2.20.6 OR 2.21.* OR 2.22.0)))
APPLICATION
| inputlookup assets_software | where like(software_name,"%n8n%") | rex field=software_version "(?<major>\d+)\.(?<minor>\d+)\.(?<patch>\d+)" | eval major=tonumber(major), minor=tonumber(minor), patch=tonumber(patch) | eval vulnerable=case( major==1 AND (minor<123 OR (minor==123 AND patch<43)), "yes-1.x", major==2 AND minor>=0 AND minor<=19, "yes-2.0-2.19", major==2 AND minor==20 AND patch<7, "yes-2.20.<7", major==2 AND minor==21, "yes-2.21", major==2 AND minor==22 AND patch<1, "yes-2.22.0", true(), "no") | where vulnerable!="no" | table host software_name software_version vulnerable

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-44789")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-44789")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve

| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities

Ongoing exploitation of Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN vulnerabilities

Cisco Talos
2026-05-14 9 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Inbound exploit attempt to Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager from known UAT-8616 / Cluster IPs · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Ongoing exploitation of Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN vulnerabilities
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] XenShell / Godzilla / Behinder JSP webshell file write on Cisco SD-WAN Manager · [LLM] AdaptixC2 'systemd-resolved' or Sliver 'CWan' implant on Linux / SD-WAN host
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] AdaptixC2 'shadowcore' / Mythic C2 traffic to UAT-8616 infrastructure 194.163.175.135 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

Inbound exploit attempt to Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager from known UAT-8616 / Cluster IPs AIExploitation Medium
Detects network connections from the Talos-published exploit-source IPs targeting Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager / vSmart (vManage) management interfaces. Anchors on the specific source IPs Talos attributes to UAT-8616 and Clusters 1-4 exploiting CVE-2026-20182 and the CVE-2026-20133/20128/20122 chain. Rationale: Source IPs are explicitly attributed by Talos to UAT-8616 (CVE-2026-20182) and Clusters 1-4 (CVE-2026-20133/20128/20122). Ports cover vManage HTTPS (443/8443), NETCONF (830), SD-WAN device control (4566), and SSH (22). Cross-checked with Cisco PSIRT advisory cisco-sa-sdwan-auth-bypass and Rapid7's disclosure referenced in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/publicationListing.x • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/sd-wan-ongoing-exploitation/
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal red-team / Rapid7 / Talos researcher scans from these IPs (rare)
  • Cisco TAC remote-assist sessions originating from Cisco-owned space (not these IPs but operationally similar)
  • Threat-intel sandbox detonations from a SOAR or VirusTotal/Hybrid-Analysis sensor on the perimeter
  • Legitimate SD-WAN partner / managed-service-provider connections routed through the same upstream ISP CIDR
Suppression filter
| where not(DestinationHostName has_any ("sandbox","honeypot","redteam"))
Response runbook
Triage: confirm the destination is a Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager/Controller and pull vManage audit logs around the connection time looking for new admin sessions, SSH key additions, or NETCONF edit-config calls. Contain: block the source IP at the perimeter, force re-authentication for the affected vManage instance, snapshot the device for forensics, and verify patch status against CVE-2026-20182/20133/20128/20122. Hunt: pivot on the device for JSP file writes (sysv.jsp, conf.jsp, sysinit.jsp, vmurnp_ikp.jsp, 20251117022131.jsp), outbound connections to 194.163.175.135 / 23.27.143.170, and processes containing /tmp/moneroocean/miner.sh.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

XenShell / Godzilla / Behinder JSP webshell file write on Cisco SD-WAN Manager AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the specific JSP webshell filenames Talos observed dropped on compromised Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager nodes after exploitation of CVE-2026-20133/20128/20122. Filenames are non-generic and attacker-chosen (20251117022131.jsp, conf.jsp, sysv.jsp, sysinit.jsp, vmurnp_ikp.jsp). Rationale: Filenames 20251117022131.jsp, conf.jsp, sysv.jsp, sysinit.jsp, vmurnp_ikp.jsp are explicitly named by Talos as attacker-dropped XenShell/Godzilla/Behinder variants on the SD-WAN Manager. Generic .jsp creation under vManage webapps directories also catches XenShell variants with rotating names since SD-WAN Manager should not be receiving developer-dropped JSPs in production. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/sd-wan-ongoing-exploitation/ • https://github.com/BeichenDream/Godzilla
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cisco-supplied upgrade package (.tar.gz) extracting legitimate vendor JSPs during a planned vManage software update
  • Backup/restore operations re-laying webapp content
  • Developer / lab vManage where engineers stage custom JSPs (should not exist in production)
  • WAR file redeployment after a TAC support case
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("tar","gzip","unzip","rpm","dpkg") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("vmanage-upgrade","viptela"))
Response runbook
Triage: read the file contents — XenShell and Godzilla shells contain recognisable Base64 payload-decryption logic and parameter-driven cmd execution; capture file hash and compare against published Godzilla/Behinder/XenShell signatures. Contain: quarantine the file, kill the Tomcat/Java process serving the webapp, isolate the SD-WAN Manager from the data-plane, and force admin credential rotation. Hunt: pull access logs for POST requests to the JSP path, pivot on source IPs (look for the cluster IPs listed in UC #1), check for follow-on Bash command execution, SSH key additions in /home/*/.ssh/authorized_keys, and outbound traffic to 194.163.175.135 / 23.27.143.170.
let WebshellNames = dynamic(["20251117022131.jsp","conf.jsp","sysv.jsp","sysinit.jsp","vmurnp_ikp.jsp"]);

   or (FileName endswith ".jsp" and FolderPath has_any ("/vmanage/","/webapps/","/opt/web-app/","/tomcat/webapps/"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

AdaptixC2 'shadowcore' / Mythic C2 traffic to UAT-8616 infrastructure 194.163.175.135 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound traffic to the AdaptixC2/Mythic infrastructure Talos attributes to UAT-8616 — IP 194.163.175.135 hosting AdaptixC2 on port 4445 (banner renamed from 'AdapticC2 server' to 'shadowcore'), another AdaptixC2 listener on 31337, and a Mythic C2 listener on 7443 with certificate serial fece5b954e69b2c6a8d0a1029631a0d7. Rationale: 194.163.175.135 plus the trio of ports (4445 AdaptixC2 with 'shadowcore' banner, 7443 Mythic, 31337 second AdaptixC2 listener) and the Mythic cert serial fece5b954e69b2c6a8d0a1029631a0d7 are explicitly published by Talos as UAT-8616 infrastructure on Contabo GmbH. The IP-and-port tuple is high-fidelity because legitimate enterprise traffic to a Contabo VPS on these obscure ports is exceedingly rare. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/sd-wan-ongoing-exploitation/ • https://github.com/Adaptix-Framework/AdaptixC2 • https://github.com/its-a-feature/Mythic
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573.002 T1095
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Certificates.All_Certificates

  • Internal red-team using a leased Contabo VPS at the same IP (verify with Red Team calendar)
  • Threat-intel detonation / sandbox call-out from a security-research host
  • Pen-test engagement where the tester reused public AdaptixC2 infrastructure (rare — most rotate)
  • Researcher running adversary-emulation labs that happen to point at the same C2
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("curl","wget") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("redteam","pentest"))
Response runbook
Triage: identify the initiating process and parent on the source host; correlate against the cert serial fece5b954e69b2c6a8d0a1029631a0d7 in TLS / Zeek x509 logs; confirm whether the source is a Cisco SD-WAN Manager. Contain: block 194.163.175.135 at the perimeter (all ports), isolate the source host, capture memory and a process tree dump. Hunt: pivot to other Contabo /24 neighbours, search for the AdaptixC2 'shadowcore' banner string in Zeek/Suricata SSL logs across 30d, and for Mythic JARM/JA3 fingerprints; check for additional post-compromise actions (SSH key writes, NETCONF edits, /tmp/moneroocean/miner.sh).

AdaptixC2 'systemd-resolved' or Sliver 'CWan' implant on Linux / SD-WAN host AIInstallation Medium
Detects the specific implant filenames Talos observed dropped post-exploitation on Cisco SD-WAN devices: 'systemd-resolved' (AdaptixC2 agent masquerading as the legitimate Linux service) calling 194.163.175.135:4445, and 'CWan' (Sliver implant) calling mtls://23.27.143.170:443. Hunts both the file presence and the C2 callouts. Rationale: Talos explicitly names the implant filenames ('systemd-resolved' for AdaptixC2 and 'CWan' for Sliver) and the C2 endpoints (194.163.175.135:4445, mtls://23.27.143.170:443). The masquerade check excludes the legitimate /lib/systemd path for systemd-resolved, so any other path equals a high-fidelity hit. Verified Sliver and AdaptixC2 framework attribution via the public AdaptixC2 and Sliver project pages. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/sd-wan-ongoing-exploitation/ • https://github.com/BishopFox/sliver • https://github.com/Adaptix-Framework/AdaptixC2
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1059.004 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A patched/upgraded systemd package temporarily executing systemd-resolved from /tmp during install (rare, vendor-signed)
  • Custom systemd build by an internal platform team installing to a non-standard path (verify with platform owner)
  • Sliver red-team engagement using the default 'CWan' name (extremely unlikely — operators rename)
  • Sysadmin script that legitimately greps log lines for 23.27.143.170 / 194.163.175.135 (extremely unlikely without prior alert)
Response runbook
Triage: capture file hash, dump memory of the process, check parent (likely tomcat / jsp shell -> bash). Contain: kill the process, quarantine the binary, isolate the host from the network, and block 194.163.175.135 and 23.27.143.170 at the perimeter. Hunt: review /home/*/.ssh/authorized_keys for new keys, NETCONF edit-config audit logs on vManage/vSmart, /tmp/moneroocean/ presence, and other hosts beaconing to either C2 IP across the last 90 days.
let C2_IPs = dynamic(["194.163.175.135","23.27.143.170"]);
let ImpostorPaths = dynamic(["/lib/systemd/systemd-resolved","/usr/lib/systemd/systemd-resolved","/usr/libexec/systemd/systemd-resolved"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
  | where (FileName =~ "systemd-resolved" and FolderPath !in~ (ImpostorPaths))
     or FileName =~ "CWan"
     or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("194.163.175.135","23.27.143.170")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AccountName),
(DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
  | where RemoteIP in (C2_IPs)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName)
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2_IPs = dynamic(["194.163.175.135","23.27.143.170"]);
let KeywordList = dynamic(["systemd-resolved","CWan","194.163.175.135","23.27.143.170","mtls://23.27.143.170"]);
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any (KeywordList)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UAT-8616 post-compromise on SD-WAN: SSH key add, NETCONF edit, su root, XMRig miner.sh AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the specific post-compromise actions Talos lists for UAT-8616 after exploitation of CVE-2026-20182/20127 — adding SSH keys, modifying NETCONF configuration, privilege escalation via 'su root -c id', plus Cluster 7's XMRig deployment via /tmp/moneroocean/miner.sh with config_background.json. Rationale: Anchors directly on the article's verbatim strings: Code Block 2 (/tmp/moneroocean/miner.sh --config=/tmp/moneroocean/config_background.json), Code Block 3 (su root -c id), and the named post-compromise actions Talos lists for UAT-8616 (SSH key addition, NETCONF configuration modification). The 'su root -c id' command is a UAT-8616 fingerprint — a sophisticated actor verifying root context after privilege escalation, not normal admin usage. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/sd-wan-ongoing-exploitation/ • https://moneroocean.stream/
ATT&CKT1098.004 T1543 T1548.003 T1496
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin running 'ssh-copy-id' or a configuration-management tool (Ansible authorized_key module, Salt ssh_auth.present) — these will hit the authorized_keys filter
  • Cisco vManage operators legitimately using NETCONF edit-config for device template pushes
  • An internal Monero mining lab (unlikely in enterprise; if present, exclude by host group)
  • Custom shell scripts that legitimately invoke 'su root -c <cmd>' on appliances during change windows
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("ansible","salt-minion","puppet","chef-client") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ssh-copy-id"))
Response runbook
Triage: identify the parent process — legitimate sysadmin work has an interactive shell ancestor; UAT-8616 activity has tomcat/jsp/sh ancestors from the webshell. Pull the user account, source IP of any preceding SSH/HTTP session, and check vManage audit logs for the corresponding NETCONF transaction ID. Contain: rotate all SSH keys for affected users, revoke unauthorized authorized_keys entries, kill miner processes, remove /tmp/moneroocean/, snapshot the device. Hunt: pivot on the parent chain back to the JSP webshell drop (UC #2), source IPs (UC #1), and outbound to AdaptixC2/Sliver C2 (UC #3, #4); search 90d for the moneroocean.stream domain and pool addresses in DNS logs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "su root" and ProcessCommandLine has "-c" and ProcessCommandLine has "id")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/tmp/moneroocean/miner.sh","config_background.json","moneroocean")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "authorized_keys" and FileName in~ ("bash","sh","tee","echo","cat","dd","cp"))
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "edit-config" and ProcessCommandLine has "netconf")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let Keywords = dynamic(["su root -c id","su root \u2013c id","/tmp/moneroocean/miner.sh","config_background.json","moneroocean","authorized_keys","edit-config","netconf"]);
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any (Keywords)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, Facility, SeverityLevel, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:(linux.auditd OR linux.syslog) (@process.command_line:(*"su root"*"-c"*id* OR *"/tmp/moneroocean/miner.sh"* OR *config_background.json* OR *moneroocean*) OR (@process.command_line:*authorized_keys* AND @process.name:(bash OR sh OR tee OR echo OR cat OR dd OR cp)) OR (@process.command_line:*edit-config* AND @process.command_line:*netconf*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | (regex("su\\s+root\\s+-c\\s+id", field=CommandLine) OR regex("/tmp/moneroocean/miner\\.sh", field=CommandLine) OR regex("config_background\\.json", field=CommandLine) OR (regex("authorized_keys", field=CommandLine) AND ImageFileName=/\/(bash|sh|tee|echo|cat|dd|cp)$/i) OR (regex("edit-config", field=CommandLine) AND regex("netconf", field=CommandLine))) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

FlowiseAI POST /api/v1/node-custom-function with NodeVM Sandbox-Escape Payload (CVE-2026-46442) AIExploitation High
Hunts authenticated POST requests to the unprotected Flowise custom-function endpoint that carry the specific NodeVM-escape payload markers documented in CVE-2026-46442 (constructor.constructor, getBuiltinModule, child_process, execSync, error.name=Object.create). High fidelity because the URL is article-specific and the payload tokens are the exact escape primitive. Rationale: Three article-specific anchors: the exact endpoint path /api/v1/node-custom-function, the JSON body field name javascriptFunction, and the documented escape primitive (constructor.constructor / getBuiltinModule / child_process). The URL is unique to Flowise; the body markers are the exact NodeVM-escape technique cited in the GHSA. Cross-checked against the @flowiseai/nodevm fork and prior vm2 sandbox-escape literature (Semgrep, BleepingComputer). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9rvc-vf7m-pgm2 • https://github.com/FlowiseAI/nodevm • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/calling-back-to-vm2-and-escaping-sandbox/ • https://www.npmjs.com/package/@flowiseai/nodevm
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007 T1068
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Flowise developers authoring legitimate Custom JS Function nodes via the UI (legit POSTs but with non-malicious bodies — no constructor.constructor / child_process markers)
  • CI/CD pipelines that deploy chatflow definitions and hit the endpoint as part of integration tests
  • Internal red-team exercises exploring the disclosed CVE before patching
  • Penetration-test scans using the public PoC against an isolated lab instance
  • Vendor-sourced WAF probes hitting the URL for fingerprinting without exploit payload
Suppression filter
// Suppress when the URL is hit WITHOUT any of the escape-payload markers AND the requester is a known admin/dev account
| where Message has_any ("constructor.constructor", "getBuiltinModule", "child_process", "Object.create(null)")
   or SourceUserName !in~ ("flowise-admin", "flowise-deployer", "ci-flowise")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Pull the full POST body from WAF/proxy archives and confirm presence of NodeVM escape markers (constructor.constructor, getBuiltinModule, child_process, execSync). Identify source IP, the Authorization header used, and any user/API key tied to the session. Step 2 — Contain: If exploit payload confirmed, isolate the Flowise host (NSG block on the source IP and outbound), rotate ALL secrets the Flowise process can read (.env, model API keys, DB creds), invalidate the API key/session used, and force upgrade to Flowise > 3.1.1 or set E2B_APIKEY to force the external sandbox path. Step 3 — Hunt: Pivot to UC2 (Flowise node.exe spawning shell). Search 30 days back for ALL hits on this endpoint to identify earlier exploitation; review outbound DNS/IP from the Flowise host for C2 indicators; check for filesystem persistence under the Flowise install directory.
// IIS / App Service in front of Flowise (URL pivot — most reverse proxies don't log POST body)
let ProxyHits =
    W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where csMethod =~ "POST"
    | where csUriStem has "/api/v1/node-custom-function"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, cIP, csUserName, csUserAgent, scStatus, sPort;
// WAF / proxy that DOES log body or the request URL with payload markers
let WafHits =
    CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
    | where RequestURL has "/api/v1/node-custom-function"
       or Message has_any ("constructor.constructor", "getBuiltinModule", "javascriptFunction", "child_process")
    | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, Message, DeviceAction;
union isfuzzy=true ProxyHits, WafHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Flowise node.exe Spawning OS Shell or Command-Line Utility - Post-Exploit RCE (CVE-2026-46442) AIExploitation High
Detects the Flowise Node.js host process spawning a child shell or built-in OS utility (cmd, powershell, sh, bash, wmic, whoami, id, hostname, ipconfig) - the exact post-conditions of the documented NodeVM escape that calls child_process.execSync. The PoC literally runs 'id' as the validation payload. Rationale: The PoC in the advisory ends with cp.execSync('id') - guaranteeing node.exe forks a shell/utility. Parent=node.exe + parent-cmd contains flowise/packages/server + child=shell-or-recon is a combination that should never occur during normal Flowise operation; the application is a JS chatflow engine, not a process orchestrator. Pivot is high-fidelity because the parent context is article-specific. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9rvc-vf7m-pgm2 • https://github.com/FlowiseAI/nodevm • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/calling-back-to-vm2-and-escaping-sandbox/
ATT&CKT1059 T1059.003 T1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Flowise LangChain Shell Tool / Bash Tool nodes - if explicitly enabled by an admin, these legitimately spawn /bin/sh or cmd.exe (rare in production deployments)
  • Flowise health-check scripts that shell out to system utilities (some Docker images include healthcheck calls to curl/wget)
  • Developer running Flowise locally with debugger attached and ad-hoc child_process calls during plugin testing
  • npm install/postinstall hooks running during a Flowise upgrade that briefly run shell commands as a child of node
  • Monitoring agents (e.g. Datadog Node tracer) that exec utilities for diagnostic data collection
Suppression filter
// Exclude known Flowise shell-tool node usage and npm install/upgrade scenarios
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install", "npm ci", "yarn install", "pnpm install", "postinstall"))
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "healthcheck" and FileName in~ ("curl.exe", "wget.exe", "curl", "wget"))
| where not (AccountName in~ ("flowise-dev", "dev-debug") and DeviceName has_any ("-dev", "-staging"))
Response runbook
Step 1 - Triage: Capture full ProcessCommandLine of the child and the parent node command line. Match against the CVE-2026-46442 PoC signature ('id', 'uname', 'whoami', or unusual recon commands). Correlate timestamp with UC1 web hits to confirm the API trigger. Step 2 - Contain: Snapshot the Flowise host, kill the Flowise process, block egress from the host at the network layer, rotate every secret the Flowise process had access to (env vars, .env file, mounted secrets, mounted API keys). Force-upgrade Flowise > 3.1.1 OR set E2B_APIKEY so subsequent code goes through the E2B external sandbox. Step 3 - Hunt: Pull DeviceFileEvents and DeviceNetworkEvents for the Flowise host going back 30 days; look for outbound C2, dropped binaries under the Flowise install path, cron / systemd / Run-key persistence written by node.exe, and any subsequent service-account credential use originating from the host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("flowise", "packages/server", "packages\\server", "@flowiseai")
     or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("flowise", "Flowise", "@flowiseai")
| where FileName in~ (
    "cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
    "wmic.exe","whoami.exe","hostname.exe","ipconfig.exe","net.exe",
    "net1.exe","netstat.exe","tasklist.exe","systeminfo.exe","reg.exe",
    "sh","bash","dash","zsh","id","uname","ifconfig","ip","ps",
    "curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat"
  )
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// Windows 4688 view
let WinHits =
    SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where ParentProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
    | where ParentProcessName has_any ("flowise", "Flowise", "@flowiseai", "packages\\server")
         or CommandLine has_any ("flowise", "Flowise")
    | where NewProcessName has_any (
        "\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe",
        "\\wmic.exe","\\whoami.exe","\\hostname.exe","\\ipconfig.exe","\\net.exe",
        "\\reg.exe","\\tasklist.exe","\\systeminfo.exe","\\curl.exe")
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
              ParentProcessName, SubjectUserName;
// Linux / ASIM view
let LinuxHits =
    ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ParentProcessName endswith "/node" or ParentProcessName == "node"
    | where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("flowise", "packages/server", "@flowiseai")
    | where TargetProcessName endswith_cs "/sh"
         or TargetProcessName endswith_cs "/bash"
         or TargetProcessName endswith_cs "/dash"
         or TargetProcessName endswith_cs "/zsh"
         or TargetProcessName in ("id","uname","whoami","hostname","ifconfig","ip","ps","curl","wget","nc","ncat")
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
              TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine,
              ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine;
union isfuzzy=true WinHits, LinuxHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Strapi CVE-2026-27886 exploit — `where[admin-relation][private-field]` query parameter against public Content API AIExploitation High
Detects HTTP requests that abuse Strapi's relational filtering bug (CVE-2026-27886) by traversing `updatedBy`/`createdBy`/`publishedBy` joins into the `admin_users` table to read private fields such as `resetPasswordToken`, `email`, or `password`. The query parameter shape is unique to this vulnerability and rarely produced by legitimate clients. Rationale: Uses the exact malicious query-parameter regex published in the GHSA advisory (`where[updatedBy|createdBy|publishedBy][resetPasswordToken|password|email|...][$startsWith|...]=`). This shape is unique to the CVE-2026-27886 exploit chain — legitimate Strapi clients filter by content-type fields, never by admin-relation private fields. corroborated_sources field references the GHSA primary source. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjg2-95x7-8qmx
ATT&CKT1190 T1212
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised penetration test against the Strapi deployment exercising this very query parameter to confirm patch level
  • Internal security-team validation of the 5.37.0 patch fix using the same payload
  • Bug bounty researcher hitting a staging instance with the disclosed PoC
  • Defensive code-scanning tools (e.g. Snyk Code) that embed CVE PoCs as canaries
  • Strapi engineering regression tests against an internal copy of the vulnerable code path
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("<pen-test-ip>", "<security-team-ip>") and HttpHostName !in ("strapi-staging.example.com", "strapi-qa.example.com")
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull all requests from the source IP in the prior 60 minutes; check whether ANY of them returned non-zero `scBytes`/200 status — a successful 200 with this query shape confirms the oracle worked. Confirm the Strapi version (`@strapi/strapi` package.json or admin footer) is <5.37.0. 2. Contain: block the source IP at the perimeter (WAF/CDN/ingress), force-rotate ALL admin password-reset tokens by clearing `admin_users.resetPasswordToken` in the database, invalidate active admin sessions, and rotate JWT secrets. 3. Hunt: search the prior 7 days of access logs for the same regex from any IP; check `POST /admin/reset-password` calls in the same window; review `admin_users.password` changes since the earliest exploit attempt to identify takeover candidates.
let LookbackHours = 24h;
let StrapiExploitRegex = @"(?i)where\[(updatedBy|createdBy|publishedBy)\]\[(email|password|resetPasswordToken|confirmationToken|firstname|lastname|preferedLanguage)\]\[\$(startsWith|contains|eq|gt|lt|ge|le|in|notIn|notNull|null)\]=";
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImWebSession
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
   | where Url matches regex StrapiExploitRegex
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, UA = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, Src = "ImWebSession"),
  (W3CIISLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
   | where csUriQuery matches regex StrapiExploitRegex
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr = cIP, HttpHostName = sSiteName, HttpMethod = csMethod, Url = strcat(csUriStem, "?", csUriQuery), HttpStatusCode = tostring(scStatus), UA = csUserAgent, Src = "W3CIISLog"),
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
   | where RequestURL matches regex StrapiExploitRegex
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr = SourceIP, HttpHostName = DestinationHostName, HttpMethod = RequestMethod, Url = RequestURL, HttpStatusCode = tostring(EventOutcome), UA = RequestClientApplication, Src = "CommonSecurityLog")
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Strapi CVE-2026-27886 Relational Filter Boolean-Oracle Exploit
id: 8a3c8e9d-7b5f-4c2a-9e1d-6f4b2c5a8e1f
status: experimental
description: Detects exploitation of CVE-2026-27886 in Strapi <5.37.0 via the `where[admin-relation][private-field][$op]=` query parameter on publicly-accessible Content API endpoints. Used to oracle-extract admin reset tokens from the admin_users table.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjg2-95x7-8qmx
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/20
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1212
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.credential_access
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_relation:
    cs-uri-query|contains:
      - 'where[updatedBy]['
      - 'where[createdBy]['
      - 'where[publishedBy]['
  selection_private_field:
    cs-uri-query|contains:
      - 'resetPasswordToken'
      - 'confirmationToken'
      - '[password]['
      - '[email]['
      - '[firstname]['
      - '[lastname]['
      - '[preferedLanguage]['
  condition: selection_relation and selection_private_field
falsepositives:
  - Authorised penetration testing or bug-bounty research against a Strapi instance
  - Internal QA tooling exercising the relational filter API
level: high
(source:nginx OR source:apache OR source:iis OR source:strapi OR source:nodejs) (@http.url_details.queryString:*where\[updatedBy\]* OR @http.url_details.queryString:*where\[createdBy\]* OR @http.url_details.queryString:*where\[publishedBy\]*) (@http.url_details.queryString:*resetPasswordToken* OR @http.url_details.queryString:*confirmationToken* OR @http.url_details.queryString:*\[password\]\[* OR @http.url_details.queryString:*\[email\]\[*)
WEB

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.uri_query) as queries values(Web.url) as urls values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents values(Web.status) as statuses from datamodel=Web where (Web.uri_query="*where[updatedBy]*" OR Web.uri_query="*where[createdBy]*" OR Web.uri_query="*where[publishedBy]*") by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.uri_path, Web.http_method | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eval is_strapi_exploit=if(match(queries, "where\[(updatedBy|createdBy|publishedBy)\]\[(email|password|resetPasswordToken|confirmationToken|firstname|lastname|preferedLanguage)\]\[\$(startsWith|contains|eq|gt|lt|ge|le|in|notIn|notNull|null)\]="), 1, 0) | where is_strapi_exploit=1 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | table firstTime, lastTime, src, dest, uri_path, http_method, queries, user_agents, statuses, count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.uri_query) as queries values(Web.url) as urls values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents values(Web.status) as statuses from datamodel=Web where (Web.uri_query="*where[updatedBy]*" OR Web.uri_query="*where[createdBy]*" OR Web.uri_query="*where[publishedBy]*") by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.uri_path, Web.http_method | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eval is_strapi_exploit=if(match(queries, "where\[(updatedBy|createdBy|publishedBy)\]\[(email|password|resetPasswordToken|confirmationToken|firstname|lastname|preferedLanguage)\]\[\$(startsWith|contains|eq|gt|lt|ge|le|in|notIn|notNull|null)\]="), 1, 0) | where is_strapi_exploit=1 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | table firstTime, lastTime, src, dest, uri_path, http_method, queries, user_agents, statuses, count
Strapi boolean-oracle hex-alphabet brute force from single source AIExploitation High
Detects the high-volume single-source brute-force pattern characteristic of CVE-2026-27886 oracle extraction: the same Content API endpoint hit dozens-to-hundreds of times from one IP with identical-shape `where[adminRel][field][$op]=<hex>` query strings where only the trailing filter value varies across the hex alphabet (`0`–`f`). Threshold-and-cardinality detection. Rationale: The article's IoC list explicitly calls out: 'High volume of public Content API requests from a single IP iterating through a hex alphabet (0-9, a-f) on the same content-type endpoint with progressively-longer filter values' and 'Sustained burst of identical-shape requests with only the trailing character of the filter value varying'. The detection codifies that — high request count + ≥16 distinct hex filter values + tight time window — into a threshold trigger. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjg2-95x7-8qmx
ATT&CKT1212 T1190 T1110.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Performance/load testing exercising parameterised filters against a Strapi staging environment
  • Internal full-content scrape using progressive filter pagination (rare with this exact query shape)
  • Web crawler aggressively enumerating a public-facing Content API
  • Bug-bounty automation re-running the disclosed PoC for variant fingerprinting
  • Internal QA executing the CVE PoC as a patch-verification canary
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("<known-loadtest-ip>", "<pen-test-ip>") and HttpHostName !endswith "staging.example.com" and HttpHostName !endswith "qa.example.com"
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the volume + cardinality matches the oracle shape — check whether each request differs only in the trailing filter value and whether the response sizes alternate (the boolean oracle signature). Identify which admin field is being oracled from the `[field]` substring (resetPasswordToken is the worst-case). 2. Contain: block the source IP at the perimeter immediately, force-clear `admin_users.resetPasswordToken` for all admin accounts, invalidate admin sessions, and verify the Strapi instance is patched to ≥5.37.0. 3. Hunt: pivot on the source IP (and User-Agent if rotated) for the prior 30 days; look for `POST /admin/reset-password` from the same or correlated IPs; review recent admin password changes that did not originate from a known internal address.
let LookbackHours = 6h;
let MinRequestsPerSource = 50;
let MinDistinctFilterValues = 16;  // hex alphabet width: 0-9,a-f
let MaxDurationSec = 1800;          // burst must be tight (~30 min) to count as oracle
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
| where Url matches regex @"(?i)where\[(updatedBy|createdBy|publishedBy)\]\[(email|password|resetPasswordToken|confirmationToken|firstname|lastname|preferedLanguage)\]\[\$"
| extend FilterValue = extract(@"(?i)where\[\w+\]\[\w+\]\[\$\w+\]=([0-9a-fA-F]+)", 1, Url)
| extend FilterFieldTuple = extract(@"(?i)(where\[\w+\]\[\w+\]\[\$\w+\])=", 1, Url)
| where isnotempty(FilterValue)
| summarize
    RequestCount   = count(),
    DistinctValues = dcount(FilterValue),
    SampleValues   = make_set(FilterValue, 20),
    DistinctTuples = dcount(FilterFieldTuple),
    SampleTuples   = make_set(FilterFieldTuple, 5),
    UAs            = make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, 5),
    FirstSeen      = min(TimeGenerated),
    LastSeen       = max(TimeGenerated)
    by SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName
| extend DurationSec = datetime_diff('second', LastSeen, FirstSeen)
| where RequestCount >= MinRequestsPerSource and DistinctValues >= MinDistinctFilterValues and DurationSec <= MaxDurationSec
| order by RequestCount desc
(source:nginx OR source:apache OR source:iis OR source:strapi OR source:nodejs) (@http.url_details.queryString:*where\[updatedBy\]* OR @http.url_details.queryString:*where\[createdBy\]* OR @http.url_details.queryString:*where\[publishedBy\]*) @http.url_details.queryString:*\$startsWith* OR @http.url_details.queryString:*\$contains* OR @http.url_details.queryString:*\$eq*
WEB

Strapi CVE-2026-27886 admin takeover — exploit burst followed by `/admin/reset-password` POST AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates a burst of CVE-2026-27886 oracle-extraction requests against a Strapi host with a subsequent `POST /admin/reset-password` call on the same host within 30 minutes. This is the closing move of the documented account-takeover chain: oracle-extract a reset token, then call the admin reset-password endpoint with it. Rationale: The article's IoC list specifies two final-stage signals: 'Subsequent POST /admin/reset-password calls using a reset token that the legitimate admin did not request' and 'Successful admin password change immediately following a burst of public Content API requests with where[updatedBy] query parameters'. The detection chains them at the per-host level with a 30-minute follow-on window — the same shape as the documented end-to-end takeover. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjg2-95x7-8qmx
ATT&CKT1078 T1212 T1098
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin legitimately requesting a password reset minutes after a pen-tester exercised the disclosed PoC on the same host
  • Coordinated red-team exercise running the full exploit chain end-to-end
  • Bug-bounty reporter demonstrating the full proof-of-concept to validate the GHSA report
  • Strapi engineering re-running their own regression test for the patch on staging
  • Migration tooling that triggers `/admin/reset-password` shortly after import scripts hit Content API filters
Suppression filter
| where ResetSrcIp !in ("<pen-test-ip>", "<security-team-ip>") and HttpHostName !endswith "staging.example.com" and not (ExploitSrcIPs has_any ("<pen-test-ip>", "<security-team-ip>"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the full request log for the target host across the chain window; identify which admin account's `resetPasswordToken` was oracled (look at `[resetPasswordToken][$startsWith]` progression) and which account received the `POST /admin/reset-password`. Cross-check whether the legitimate admin actually requested a reset (Slack/ticket/HR system). 2. Contain: assume admin compromise — disable the targeted admin account, force-rotate ALL admin credentials and reset tokens, rotate `JWT_SECRET` and `ADMIN_JWT_SECRET` in Strapi config, invalidate active sessions, block the source IP(s), and snapshot the database for forensics before remediation. Upgrade to ≥5.37.0 before re-enabling admin accounts. 3. Hunt: trawl the prior 30 days for the same exploit regex on this host AND every other Strapi host in the estate; review `admin_users` audit history for unauthorised additions or role changes; check for new API tokens created by the targeted admin account post-reset; pivot on attacker
let LookbackHours = 24h;
let ChainWindow   = 30min;
let MinExploitReqs = 10;
let StrapiExploitRegex = @"(?i)where\[(updatedBy|createdBy|publishedBy)\]\[(email|password|resetPasswordToken|confirmationToken|firstname|lastname|preferedLanguage)\]\[\$";
let ExploitBursts =
    ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
    | where Url matches regex StrapiExploitRegex
    | summarize ExploitCount = count(), FirstExploit = min(TimeGenerated), LastExploit = max(TimeGenerated), ExploitSrcIPs = make_set(SrcIpAddr, 10) by HttpHostName
    | where ExploitCount >= MinExploitReqs;
let ResetCalls =
    ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
    | where Url has "/admin/reset-password"
    | where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
    | project ResetTime = TimeGenerated, ResetHost = HttpHostName, ResetSrcIp = SrcIpAddr, ResetUrl = Url, ResetUA = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent;
ExploitBursts
| join kind=inner ResetCalls on $left.HttpHostName == $right.ResetHost
| where ResetTime between (FirstExploit .. (LastExploit + ChainWindow))
| extend ChainLatencySec = datetime_diff('second', ResetTime, LastExploit)
| project FirstExploit, LastExploit, ResetTime, ChainLatencySec, HttpHostName, ExploitCount, ExploitSrcIPs, ResetSrcIp, ResetUrl, ResetUA
| order by ResetTime desc
(source:nginx OR source:apache OR source:iis OR source:strapi OR source:nodejs) ((@http.url_details.queryString:*where\[updatedBy\]* OR @http.url_details.queryString:*where\[createdBy\]* OR @http.url_details.queryString:*where\[publishedBy\]*) OR (@http.url_details.path:*/admin/reset-password @http.method:POST))
