Vulnerable Amazon Redshift JDBC Driver (CVE-2026-8178) inventory hunt — redshift-jdbc42 < 2.2.2 AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces every host/asset where Defender TVM (or equivalent vuln scanner) reports the Amazon Redshift JDBC Driver below the patched 2.2.2 release, so the SOC can prioritise patching/segmentation of the JVMs whose classpath could be weaponised through CVE-2026-8178. Rationale: Pivots on the explicit CVE id and the affected Maven coordinate (`com.amazon.redshift:redshift-jdbc42` < 2.2.2) called out in the GHSA. Since the article confirms the fix landed in 2.2.2, the version-prefix exclusion list (2.2.2/.3/.4/.5/.6) is a precise inventory filter — false positives only when TVM lags on a freshly patched host. Joining DeviceInfo flags Internet-facing JVM hosts so the SOC can sequence patching by exposure. Datadog left blank because TVM CVE coverage is not shipped to Datadog logs in this estate; Sigma left blank because TVM is a snapshot, not an event-shaped log. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/aws/amazon-redshift-jdbc-driver/security/advisories/GHSA-wmmv-vvg5-993q • https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/rss/2026-028-aws/ • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/cve-2026-8178-cwe-470-use-of-externally-controlled-c4285304 • https://github.com/aws/amazon-redshift-jdbc-driver/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md

CVE-2026-8178 exploit attempt: Redshift JDBC URL with class-loading parameter (socketFactory/sslfactory/sslhostnameverifier/sslpasswordcallb AIExploitation High
Hunts for the specific exploit primitive of CVE-2026-8178 — a `jdbc:redshift://` connection string carrying one of the four parameters (`socketFactory`, `sslfactory`, `sslhostnameverifier`, `sslpasswordcallback`) the unpatched driver instantiates without type-checking. Surfaces the URL whether it appears in a JVM command line, a connection-string env-var passed at fork, or a webapp HTTP request that accepts user-supplied JDBC URLs (DataEase-style sink). Rationale: The four parameter names (`socketFactory`, `sslfactory`, `sslhostnameverifier`, `sslpasswordcallback`) are the documented type-confusion sinks where the unpatched driver `Class.forName()`-then-instantiates whatever class name the JDBC URL specifies — confirmed by the AWS security bulletin and the related historical advisory chain (CVE-2022-41828, CVE-2024-12744). Pairing them with the `jdbc:redshift` scheme literal and the `java.exe`/`javaw.exe` image gives a 3-of-3 high-fidelity composite that has effectively zero benign use. The web-tier branch catches the DataEase-style sink where a webapp accepts user-supplied JDBC URLs (corroborated by GHSA-mfg2-qr5c-99pp). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/aws/amazon-redshift-jdbc-driver/security/advisories/GHSA-wmmv-vvg5-993q • https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/rss/2026-028-aws/ • https://github.com/murataydemir/CVE-2022-41828 • https://github.com/dataease/dataease/security/advisories/GHSA-mfg2-qr5c-99pp • https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2024-015/

Kimsuky HelloDoor 'tdll' Run-key persistence with regsvr32 loader AIInstallation High
Hunts the autorun footprint of HelloDoor, Kimsuky's first Rust-based PebbleDash variant. HelloDoor uniquely registers itself under HKCU\...\Run with the value name 'tdll' and a data string invoking 'regsvr32.exe /s [DLL path]'. The combination of that exact value name and a regsvr32 silent-load command in a Run key is article-specific and not seen in benign software. Rationale: The article explicitly names the Run-key value 'tdll' and data 'regsvr32.exe /s [current file path]' as HelloDoor's persistence routine. 'tdll' has no documented benign use and the regsvr32 silent flag adds further specificity. Token-aligned matches on the registry path and value data make this a tight, low-FP detection. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/kimsuky-appleseed-pebbledash-campaigns/119785/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0094/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1547/001/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1218.010
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "tdll"
| where RegistryValueData has "regsvr32" and RegistryValueData has "/s"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValue =~ "tdll"
| where RegistryValueData has "regsvr32" and RegistryValueData has "/s"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Kimsuky httpMalice persistence: 'Everything 1.9a-/1.8a-' Run-key or CacheDB service install AIInstallation High
Hunts httpMalice (latest PebbleDash backdoor variant) establishing persistence. Depending on token elevation, it either creates a service named 'CacheDB' (display name 'Administrator', running 'rundll32.exe [dll path], load') or writes an HKCU Run-key value named 'Everything 1.9a-[filesize]' (or older 'Everything 1.8a-[filesize]'). Both indicators are uniquely tied to httpMalice. Rationale: The article literally names 'Everything 1.9a-[filesize]' / 'Everything 1.8a-[filesize]' as the Run-key value names httpMalice writes, and 'CacheDB' (with 'rundll32.exe [DLL], load' image path and 'Administrator' display name) as the service it creates when elevated. Both strings are bespoke to httpMalice — joining registry + service-install telemetry captures both code paths. Sigma omitted because the rule is a union of two distinct event shapes (registry value set + service install). Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/kimsuky-appleseed-pebbledash-campaigns/119785/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0094/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/003/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1543.003 T1218.011
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry Endpoint.Services
union
(DeviceRegistryEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
  | where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
  | where RegistryKey has @"\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"
  | where RegistryValueName matches regex @"(?i)^Everything 1\.[89]a-\d+$"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
            Signal = "httpMalice RunKey (Everything 1.9a-/1.8a-)",
            Detail = strcat(RegistryValueName, " => ", RegistryValueData)),
(DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
  | where ActionType == "ServiceInstalled"
  | extend AF = parse_json(AdditionalFields)
  | extend SvcName = tostring(AF.ServiceName), SvcImage = tostring(AF.ServiceFileName)
  | where SvcName =~ "CacheDB"
  | where SvcImage has "rundll32" and SvcImage has ",load"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
            Signal = "httpMalice CacheDB service install",
            Detail = SvcImage)
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(ImRegistryEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where RegistryKey has @"\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"
  | where RegistryValue matches regex @"(?i)^Everything 1\.[89]a-\d+$"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
            Signal = "httpMalice RunKey (Everything 1.9a-/1.8a-)",
            Detail = strcat(RegistryValue, " => ", RegistryValueData)),
(Event
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where EventLog == "System" and EventID == 7045
  | where RenderedDescription has "CacheDB"
  | where RenderedDescription has "rundll32" and RenderedDescription has ",load"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname = Computer, ActorUsername = UserName, ActingProcessName = "services.exe",
            Signal = "httpMalice CacheDB service install",
            Detail = RenderedDescription)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Kimsuky JSE dropper: wscript -> powershell hidden + certutil -decode chain AIDelivery High
Hunts the literal command-line emitted by Kimsuky's JSE droppers (HelloDoor, httpMalice, AppleSeed deliveries): 'powershell.exe -windowstyle hidden certutil -decode [src] [dst]'. The dropper executes via wscript.exe (default JSE handler), shells PowerShell hidden, and uses certutil to base64-decode the second-stage payload before invoking it with regsvr32/rundll32. Rationale: Direct quote from the article: 'The malicious payload leverages powershell.exe -windowstyle hidden certutil -decode [src path] [dst path] for the second Base64 decoding before execution.' JSE files are handled by wscript.exe by default. The four-token combination (windowstyle + hidden + certutil + -decode in one cmdline, parented by a script host) is essentially never seen in benign software. Defender query also chains to the follow-on regsvr32/rundll32 from C:\ProgramData mentioned in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/kimsuky-appleseed-pebbledash-campaigns/119785/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0094/ • https://lolbas-project.github.io/lolbas/Binaries/Certutil/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.005 T1140 T1564.003 T1218.010
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "powershell.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "windowstyle" and ProcessCommandLine has "hidden"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "certutil" and ProcessCommandLine has "-decode"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","explorer.exe","cmd.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName in~ ("regsvr32.exe","rundll32.exe")
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "powershell.exe"
    | where FolderPath has @"C:\ProgramData" or ProcessCommandLine has @"C:\ProgramData"
    | project FollowOnTime = Timestamp, DeviceName, FollowOnCmd = ProcessCommandLine, FollowOnFile = FileName
  ) on DeviceName
| where isnull(FollowOnTime) or FollowOnTime between (Timestamp .. Timestamp + 5m)
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith "powershell.exe"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "windowstyle" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "hidden"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "certutil" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "-decode"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","explorer.exe","cmd.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")

| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DeviceFileEvents

| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")

| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("995a0a49ae4b244928b3f67e2bfd7a6e", "52f1ff082e981cbdfd1f045c6021c63f", "65fc9f06de5603e2c1af9b4f288bb22c", "8e15c4d4f71bdd9dbc48cd2cabc87806", "8983ffa6da23e0b99ccc58c17b9788c7") or SHA1 in~ ("995a0a49ae4b244928b3f67e2bfd7a6e", "52f1ff082e981cbdfd1f045c6021c63f", "65fc9f06de5603e2c1af9b4f288bb22c", "8e15c4d4f71bdd9dbc48cd2cabc87806", "8983ffa6da23e0b99ccc58c17b9788c7") or MD5 in~ ("995a0a49ae4b244928b3f67e2bfd7a6e", "52f1ff082e981cbdfd1f045c6021c63f", "65fc9f06de5603e2c1af9b4f288bb22c", "8e15c4d4f71bdd9dbc48cd2cabc87806", "8983ffa6da23e0b99ccc58c17b9788c7")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("995a0a49ae4b244928b3f67e2bfd7a6e", "52f1ff082e981cbdfd1f045c6021c63f", "65fc9f06de5603e2c1af9b4f288bb22c", "8e15c4d4f71bdd9dbc48cd2cabc87806", "8983ffa6da23e0b99ccc58c17b9788c7") or SHA1 in~ ("995a0a49ae4b244928b3f67e2bfd7a6e", "52f1ff082e981cbdfd1f045c6021c63f", "65fc9f06de5603e2c1af9b4f288bb22c", "8e15c4d4f71bdd9dbc48cd2cabc87806", "8983ffa6da23e0b99ccc58c17b9788c7") or MD5 in~ ("995a0a49ae4b244928b3f67e2bfd7a6e", "52f1ff082e981cbdfd1f045c6021c63f", "65fc9f06de5603e2c1af9b4f288bb22c", "8e15c4d4f71bdd9dbc48cd2cabc87806", "8983ffa6da23e0b99ccc58c17b9788c7")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["995a0a49ae4b244928b3f67e2bfd7a6e", "52f1ff082e981cbdfd1f045c6021c63f", "65fc9f06de5603e2c1af9b4f288bb22c", "8e15c4d4f71bdd9dbc48cd2cabc87806", "8983ffa6da23e0b99ccc58c17b9788c7"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FrostyNeighbor PicassoLoader drop to %AppData%\WinDataScope\Update.js AIInstallation High
Hunts the article-specific second-stage drop: a JavaScript PicassoLoader payload written to a fixed AppData subfolder ('WinDataScope') used by FrostyNeighbor's March 2026 Ukrtelecom-themed compromise chain. The folder name and filename are both fingerprinted by ESET against multiple samples in this campaign. Rationale: WinDataScope is a folder name nowhere referenced in legitimate software inventories — ESET fingerprints it directly to FrostyNeighbor's PicassoLoader staging in the May 2026 report. Combined with the file name Update.js this is a near-zero-FP file-write signature. Cross-checked against: • https://cert.gov.ua/article/40240 • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1010/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/
ATT&CKT1027.009 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal red-team simulation of UNC1151 IOCs
  • Threat intel detonation labs writing the IOC to disk
  • Backup software restoring an archived Update.js artifact
  • Security researcher repository clone containing this sample
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MpCmdRun.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName =~ "system")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Hash the file (SHA-1/256) and compare to ESET's published B65551D339AECE718EA1465BF3542C794C445EFC and E15ABEE1CFDE8BE7D87C7C0B510450BAD6BC0906; pull the parent process tree (expect wscript.exe with --update arg). Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host via Defender Live Response or Falcon Network Containment; kill any wscript.exe/cscript.exe running Update.js; remove the WinDataScope folder and any scheduled tasks referencing it. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep org for additional WinDataScope folders, any DNS lookups to needbinding.icu / nebao.icu / algsat.icu / sardk.icu / alexavegas.icu / lavanille.buzz, and ViberPC.dll image loads.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Roaming\WinDataScope" and FileName =~ "Update.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA1, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName

FrostyNeighbor JS dropper self-relaunch with --update flag AIExploitation High
Detects the FrostyNeighbor first-stage JavaScript dropper's documented self-relaunch pattern: wscript.exe / cscript.exe executes a .js file with the literal '--update' argument so the second branch of the script can install PicassoLoader. The flag string is bespoke to this campaign and is not used by legitimate Windows Script Host workflows. Rationale: The article explicitly states the first-stage script re-executes itself with the --update flag to branch into the PicassoLoader drop. The double-dash --update form is uncommon in WSH-launched JavaScript and pairs with a .js argument that is rarely seen in benign workflows. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/007/ • https://cert.gov.ua/article/40240
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Bespoke Windows updater wrappers some sysadmins build using JScript
  • Vendor installers that pass --update to a side-by-side wscript helper
  • RMM tooling using JS-based updater payloads
  • Penetration test simulations referencing the same TTP
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"C:\Program Files\",@"C:\Program Files (x86)\") and InitiatingProcessFileName !endswith "explorer.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Resolve the full .js path from ProcessCommandLine — confirm whether it sits in a user-writable directory (Desktop, Downloads, Temp, %AppData%) which is the FrostyNeighbor pattern. Hash the .js and compare to ESET's published 8D1F2A6DF51C7783F2EAF1A0FC0FF8D032E5B57F. Step 2 (contain): Kill the wscript/cscript process tree; quarantine the .js; isolate host. Step 3 (hunt): Look for the parent process — the original execution should be either explorer.exe (manual double-click) or winrar.exe/7z.exe extracting from 53_7.03.2026_R.rar. Also hunt for the WinDataScope drop and outbound DNS to needbinding.icu / nebao.icu.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--update"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--update" and ActingProcessCommandLine has ".js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FrostyNeighbor C2 callout to needbinding/nebao/algsat/sardk/alexavegas/lavanille AICommand & Control High
Detects DNS or HTTP egress to the six FrostyNeighbor C2 domains published by ESET in May 2026 (PicassoLoader on five .icu hosts plus a .buzz Cobalt Strike host). All six share the same actor infrastructure cluster registered between 2026-03-10 and 2026-04-14. Rationale: ESET published the full domain list in Table 2 of the article alongside first-seen dates from a freshly-registered actor infrastructure cluster (.icu/.buzz, no legitimate corporate use). Any host in a UA/PL/LT/EE government estate touching these domains is high-fidelity actor traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1010/ • https://cert.gov.ua/article/40240
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DFIR team detonating samples in a connected analysis VM
  • Threat-intel ingestion proxies fetching the same samples
  • Researcher accessing the article and clicking through to defang links
  • Honeypot connecting to the C2 to fingerprint it
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Defender\")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the contacting process via InitiatingProcessFileName / ContextImageFileName — for wscript.exe/cscript.exe parents this is almost certainly PicassoLoader. Capture the User-Agent and full URL. Step 2 (contain): Sinkhole the domain at egress (block at firewall + DNS); isolate the host; pull memory and disk image. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the resolved IP — Cloudflare-fronted but the origin may rotate; check for sibling domains on the same naming pattern (*-*.needbinding.icu, attachment-storage-asset-static.needbinding.icu), and hunt for the WinDataScope drop and ViberPC.dll on every host that resolved any of the six domains.
let FrostyDomains = dynamic(["needbinding.icu","nebao.icu","algsat.icu","alexavegas.icu","sardk.icu","lavanille.buzz"]);
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any (FrostyDomains)
    | extend Source="NetworkEvent"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source;
let EventHits = DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
    | where ActionType =~ "DnsQueryResponse"
    | extend QueriedDomain = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).DnsQueryString)
    | where QueriedDomain has_any (FrostyDomains)
    | extend Source="DnsQuery"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP="", RemoteUrl=QueriedDomain,
              RemotePort=tolong(0),
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              InitiatingProcessAccountName=AccountName, Source;
union NetHits, EventHits
| order by Timestamp desc
let FrostyDomains = dynamic(["needbinding.icu","nebao.icu","algsat.icu","alexavegas.icu","sardk.icu","lavanille.buzz"]);
union isfuzzy=true
    (ImDnsActivity
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
        | where DnsQuery has_any (FrostyDomains)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Domain=DnsQuery, Source="DNS"),
    (ImWebSession
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
        | where Url has_any (FrostyDomains) or HttpHostName has_any (FrostyDomains)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname=SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Domain=coalesce(HttpHostName,Url), Source="HTTP"),
    (CommonSecurityLog
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
        | where RequestURL has_any (FrostyDomains) or DestinationHostName has_any (FrostyDomains)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname=SourceHostName, SrcIpAddr=SourceIP, SrcUsername=SourceUserName, Domain=coalesce(DestinationHostName,RequestURL), Source="FW")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PicassoLoader scheduled-task creation by wscript/cscript after C2 XML fetch AIInstallation Medium
Detects FrostyNeighbor's persistence step: the JavaScript dropper downloads a scheduled-task XML template (served via the misleading Content-Type/Content-Disposition response to a .jpg URL) and then registers it. The parent-child chain of WSH spawning schtasks.exe or powershell.exe Register-ScheduledTask is article-specific. Rationale: The article describes the script downloading 'https://book-happy.needbinding[.]icu/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/1GreenAM.jpg' (which actually returns config.xml with Content-Type: application/xml) and then using it for persistence. Wscript/cscript spawning schtasks /Create /XML is a tight, low-FP pivot specific to this WSH-driven persistence pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053/005/ • https://cert.gov.ua/article/40240
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Adobe / vendor installer JScript wrappers that schedule a maintenance task
  • Internal MDM scripts that register update tasks via JScript bootstrappers
  • Application Compatibility scripts during corporate imaging
  • RMM agents using a JScript first-stage that registers a service-task
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"C:\Program Files\",@"C:\Program Files (x86)\",@"C:\Windows\CCM\",@"C:\Windows\System32\GroupPolicy\") and AccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Dump the scheduled-task XML (schtasks /Query /TN <task> /XML) — the FrostyNeighbor template launches %AppData%\WinDataScope\Update.js on a schedule. Capture parent process tree back to the original .js file under the user profile. Step 2 (contain): schtasks /Delete /TN <task> /F; remove the WinDataScope folder; isolate host; pull memory. Step 3 (hunt): Across the org, look for any scheduled task whose Action.Command points into %AppData%\WinDataScope or whose RegistrationInfo.Source mentions WinDataScope; cross-reference with DNS hits on the six C2 domains.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/Create","/XML"))
      or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "Register-ScheduledTask")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ChildProcess=FileName, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcess=InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          GrandparentProcess=InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where (ActingProcessName has "schtasks.exe" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/Create","/XML"))
      or (ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ActingProcessCommandLine has "Register-ScheduledTask")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WSH-Initiated Scheduled Task Registration (FrostyNeighbor PicassoLoader)
id: 2c8f47a3-9b14-4ee5-b87e-91a4f5d63c11
description: Detects wscript.exe or cscript.exe spawning schtasks.exe /Create /XML or powershell Register-ScheduledTask. This is the persistence step in FrostyNeighbor's March 2026 PicassoLoader chain, in which an XML template is downloaded under a fake .jpg URL and registered as a scheduled task.
references:
  - https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/frostyneighbor-fresh-mischief-digital-shenanigans/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/19
tags:
  - attack.t1053.005
  - attack.t1059.007
  - attack.persistence
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:

      - '\cscript.exe'
  child_schtasks:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/Create'
      - '/XML'
  child_pwsh:
    Image|endswith:

falsepositives:

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@ParentImage:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\WScript.exe OR *\\CScript.exe OR *\\WSCRIPT.EXE OR *\\CSCRIPT.EXE)) ((@Image:(*\\schtasks.exe OR *\\SchTasks.exe OR *\\SCHTASKS.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*/Create* OR */XML*)) OR (@Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\\pwsh.exe) AND @CommandLine:*Register-ScheduledTask*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i
| (ImageFileName=/schtasks\.exe$/i AND regex("(/Create|/XML)", field=CommandLine))
  OR (ImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i AND regex("Register-ScheduledTask", field=CommandLine))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as child_cmdline values(Processes.parent_process) as parent_cmdline from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") (Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" OR (Processes.process_name="powershell.exe" AND Processes.process="*Register-ScheduledTask*") OR Processes.process_name="taskeng.exe") (Processes.process="*/Create*" OR Processes.process="*Register-ScheduledTask*" OR Processes.process="*/XML*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
FrostyNeighbor Cobalt Strike beacon ViberPC.dll image load AIInstallation Medium
Detects loading of ViberPC.dll, the final-stage Cobalt Strike beacon FrostyNeighbor masquerades as the legitimate Viber desktop messenger DLL. ESET publishes a SHA-1 (43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB) and the file is expected outside the legitimate Viber install path under the standard Cobalt Strike beacon naming pattern Win32/CobaltStrike.Beacon.S. Rationale: ESET published the exact SHA-1 (43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB) for the ViberPC.dll Cobalt Strike beacon in Table 1, classified Win32/CobaltStrike.Beacon.S. Combined with masquerading detection — ViberPC.dll loaded from a non-Viber path — this is a high-confidence final-stage beacon detection. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0154/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1010/ • https://cert.gov.ua/article/40240
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1055.001 T1588.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Viber portable install on a corporate device outside standard install paths
  • DFIR / red-team Cobalt Strike training exercise with renamed loader
  • Backup software restoring a snapshot containing the IOC
  • File-server hosting a software repository with the sample present
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\Viber\",@"\Program Files (x86)\Viber\",@"\AppData\Local\Viber\") and SHA1 !in~ ("43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Hash-verify the loaded DLL against ESET's published SHA-1; capture the loading process (often rundll32.exe, regsvr32.exe, or a sacrificial process injected by PicassoLoader). Pull memory of the loading process for beacon config extraction. Step 2 (contain): Isolate host via EDR; block hash org-wide; sinkhole nama-belakang.nebao.icu and best-seller.lavanille.buzz at egress. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all hosts for ViberPC.dll outside the Viber install path; pivot on beacon C2 IP after extracting the malleable profile; check AAD/SigninLogs for anomalous interactive logons from any host that loaded the beacon (lateral-movement indicator).
let FrostyHashes = dynamic(["43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB"]);
let ImageLoads = DeviceImageLoadEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
    | where FileName =~ "ViberPC.dll"
    | where SHA1 in~ (FrostyHashes)
         or not (FolderPath has @"\Viber\" or FolderPath has @"\Program Files\Viber")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, SHA256,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
              InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source="ImageLoad";
let FileWrites = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
    | where FileName =~ "ViberPC.dll"
    | where SHA1 in~ (FrostyHashes)
         or not (FolderPath has @"\Viber\" or FolderPath has @"\Program Files\Viber")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, SHA256,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
              InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source="FileWrite";
union ImageLoads, FileWrites
| order by Timestamp desc
let FrostyHashes = dynamic(["43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "ViberPC.dll"
| where TargetFileSHA1 in~ (FrostyHashes)
     or not (TargetFilePath has @"\Viber\" or TargetFilePath has @"\Program Files\Viber")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath,
          TargetFileSHA1, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental

references:

tags:

detection:

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("776A43E46C36A539C916ED426745EE96E2392B39", "8D1F2A6DF51C7783F2EAF1A0FC0FF8D032E5B57F", "B65551D339AECE718EA1465BF3542C794C445EFC", "43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB") or SHA1 in~ ("776A43E46C36A539C916ED426745EE96E2392B39", "8D1F2A6DF51C7783F2EAF1A0FC0FF8D032E5B57F", "B65551D339AECE718EA1465BF3542C794C445EFC", "43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB") or MD5 in~ ("776A43E46C36A539C916ED426745EE96E2392B39", "8D1F2A6DF51C7783F2EAF1A0FC0FF8D032E5B57F", "B65551D339AECE718EA1465BF3542C794C445EFC", "43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("776A43E46C36A539C916ED426745EE96E2392B39", "8D1F2A6DF51C7783F2EAF1A0FC0FF8D032E5B57F", "B65551D339AECE718EA1465BF3542C794C445EFC", "43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB") or SHA1 in~ ("776A43E46C36A539C916ED426745EE96E2392B39", "8D1F2A6DF51C7783F2EAF1A0FC0FF8D032E5B57F", "B65551D339AECE718EA1465BF3542C794C445EFC", "43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB") or MD5 in~ ("776A43E46C36A539C916ED426745EE96E2392B39", "8D1F2A6DF51C7783F2EAF1A0FC0FF8D032E5B57F", "B65551D339AECE718EA1465BF3542C794C445EFC", "43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["776A43E46C36A539C916ED426745EE96E2392B39", "8D1F2A6DF51C7783F2EAF1A0FC0FF8D032E5B57F", "B65551D339AECE718EA1465BF3542C794C445EFC", "43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Strapi Content-Type Builder Write API Reached in Production (CVE-2026-22599) AIExploitation Medium
Detects POST/PUT to Strapi's Content-Type Builder write endpoint from a non-internal source. Per the patch (v5.33.2 / v4.26.1) these endpoints are disabled outside dev mode and return 404 — any successful POST/PUT in production indicates an unpatched instance under active exploitation or pre-patch admin misuse, both worth alerting on. Rationale: Anchored to the article's primary IOC — the literal endpoint path `/content-type-builder/content-types` and the (POST|PUT) verb regex. The patch behavior (404 in production) is what makes any such request high-signal: the article explicitly states the patch 'returns 404 for requests against /content-type-builder/content-types... removing the network-reachable attack surface entirely'. Splunk filters out RFC1918/loopback to focus on internet-reachable instances; Sentinel uses ImWebSession + not(ipv4_is_private) for the same effect. Defender Advanced Hunting has no native web access-log table, so defender_kql is empty (this telemetry lives in W3CIISLog / WAF logs, not DeviceProcessEvents).
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb
// Strapi Content-Type Builder endpoint should return 404 in production (v5.33.2+/v4.26.1+)
// Any POST/PUT reaching it from a non-internal source = exploit attempt or unpatched instance
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where HttpMethod in ("POST","PUT")
| where Url contains "/content-type-builder/content-types"
| where isnotempty(SrcIpAddr)
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr))
| where not(SrcIpAddr startswith "127.")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpRequestHeaderReferer
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Strapi Content-Type Builder Write Followed by Server-Side Error (CVE-2026-22599 DoS / migration crash) AIExploitation Medium
Detects POST/PUT to the Strapi Content-Type Builder content-types endpoint that returns a 5xx status — the article's explicit IOC for exploitation is 'Strapi server crashes immediately following a content-type creation or update, observed as the Node process exiting during the schema-migration step'. A 502/503/504 (upstream Strapi unreachable) or 500 from the Strapi node itself, gated to this specific URI, is a high-fidelity DoS / migration-error signal for the isRaw raw() injection. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit behavioural IOC — 'Strapi server crashes immediately following a content-type creation or update, observed as the Node process exiting during the schema-migration step'. A failed migration manifests as a 5xx on the same HTTP transaction (500 from Strapi itself, 502/503/504 from the upstream reverse proxy after node exits), so a single-event filter on (POST|PUT) + /content-type-builder/ + status≥500 is high-fidelity and Sigma-compatible. Datadog query left empty because the standard log sources listed (cloudtrail, azure.*, windows.*, linux.*, gcp.audit, kubernetes.audit, okta) do not include a generic web-access source — this telemetry would arrive at Datadog via a custom nginx/apache source not enumerated in the schema reference. Defender has no native web-access-log table.
ATT&CKT1190 T1499.004
Data sourcesWeb
// Schema-migration crash signature for CVE-2026-22599: 5xx response to a Content-Type Builder write
// Mirrors article IOC: 'Node process exiting during the schema-migration step'
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where HttpMethod in ("POST","PUT")
| where Url contains "/content-type-builder/"
| where HttpStatusCode between (500 .. 599)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| summarize Hits = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), DistinctUrls = make_set(Url, 25), Statuses = make_set(HttpStatusCode, 10) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod
| order by LastSeen desc

SiYuan Electron renderer spawns shell/scripting child (CVE-2026-45375 Bazaar XSS → RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the post-exploit RCE step of CVE-2026-45375. The SiYuan Bazaar XSS pivots to OS command execution via Node's child_process from a renderer with nodeIntegration=true. A SiYuan main/renderer process spawning cmd/powershell/pwsh/wscript/cscript/bash/sh/osascript/open/calc is highly anomalous — SiYuan is a markdown notes app and does not legitimately invoke shells. Rationale: Direct from the article: the renderer runs with `nodeIntegration:true`, `contextIsolation:false`, `webSecurity:false` (app/electron/main.js:407-411) and the Electron RCE PoC explicitly substitutes `require('child_process').exec('open -a Calculator')` as the payload string. Any shell/scripting child of siyuan.exe is therefore the executed payload. Cross-checked against memory observation 392 (SiYuan Electron RCE CVE cluster). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-27qc-m5gf-jv5r
ATT&CKT1059 T1203 T1189

SiYuan Bazaar manifest written with embedded HTML/script markers (CVE-2026-45375 dropper) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the dropper stage of CVE-2026-45375. A malicious Bazaar package's `plugin.json` / `theme.json` / `template.json` / `widget.json` / `icon.json` carrying HTML in the unsanitized `name` or `version` fields lands in the SiYuan workspace under `data/plugins/`, `data/themes/`, etc. Honest assumption: the file is dropped by something other than siyuan.exe itself (file-system sync, archive extraction, sideload) — siyuan.exe → manifest is the legitimate marketplace path. Targets the workspace manifest pattern named by the advisory. Rationale: Article names the exact five manifest filenames (plugin.json/theme.json/template.json/widget.json/icon.json), the exact workspace layout (`/tmp/siyuan-poc-ws/data/plugins/evil-plugin/plugin.json` in the Docker PoC), and the unescaped fields (`name`, `version`). FileSize > 2048 is a heuristic — clean manifests in the wild are ~200-600 bytes; the PoC payload bloats them. Tier=hunting because content inspection would be required to confirm the HTML payload — without it some baseline noise from legitimate marketplace installs is expected. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-27qc-m5gf-jv5r
ATT&CKT1546 T1059.007

// CVE-2026-45375 — SiYuan Bazaar manifest dropped in workspace (potential payload carrier)
let _manifest_names = dynamic(["plugin.json","theme.json","template.json","widget.json","icon.json"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName in~ (_manifest_names)
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\data\plugins\", @"\data\themes\", @"\data\templates\", @"\data\widgets\", @"\data\icons\",
                            "/data/plugins/", "/data/themes/", "/data/templates/", "/data/widgets/", "/data/icons/")
// honest manifests are tiny (~200-500 bytes); HTML/JS payload bloats them, OR a non-siyuan writer = sideload
| where FileSize > 2048
   or not(InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("siyuan.exe","siyuan"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, FileSize, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
// CVE-2026-45375 — Sentinel ASIM port
let _manifest_names = dynamic(["plugin.json","theme.json","template.json","widget.json","icon.json"]);
ImFileEvent

| where TargetFileName in~ (_manifest_names)

TeamPCP's Mini Shai-Hulud Is Back: A Self-Spreading Supply Chain Attack Compromises TanStack npm Packages

2026-05-12 14 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Mini Shai-Hulud npm Worm C2 callback to Session Protocol CDN and masscan.cloud AICommand & Control High
Detects DNS resolution or outbound TCP/UDP to the Session Protocol seed nodes (seed1.getsession.org, filev2.getsession.org) and api.masscan.cloud used by TeamPCP's Mini Shai-Hulud worm to exfiltrate harvested CI/CD secrets and developer credentials. These hostnames are not part of any legitimate enterprise software supply chain and any contact is high-fidelity. Rationale: Domains seed1.getsession.org, filev2.getsession.org, and api.masscan.cloud are named explicitly as the worm's exfiltration channel in the StepSecurity write-up. Session Protocol nodes have zero legitimate enterprise use and api.masscan.cloud is the same C2 infrastructure observed across the @antv variant (memory observation 1252) — high-fidelity primary IOCs across multiple StepSecurity / Socket.dev / JFrog reports on the campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-a-self-spreading-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-npm-ecosystem • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1567/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1567 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer running the Session Messenger desktop app on a corp workstation (rare; whitelist by user)
  • Security researchers detonating the worm in an authorized sandbox host
  • Internal red team replaying campaign IOCs during a purple-team exercise
  • Threat-intel platforms (MISP, OpenCTI) performing connectivity checks against indicator URLs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("session.exe","Session.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("session.exe","Session.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Identify the InitiatingProcessFileName / ContextImageFileName — confirm it is node, npm, bun, git, or a CI runner process (and not Session Messenger). Pivot on DeviceId to list every package install in the prior 24h on that host. Step 2 (Contain): Isolate the device via Defender Live Response, force-rotate all credentials in scope (npm tokens, GitHub PATs, cloud keys, .env values), and revoke OIDC trust on the affected GitHub Actions repo. Step 3 (Hunt): Across the org, sweep DeviceFileEvents for router_init.js drops and DeviceProcessEvents for any commit authored as claude@users.noreply.github.com in the last 14d to find every laterally-infected publisher.
let CampaignHosts = dynamic(["seed1.getsession.org","filev2.getsession.org","api.masscan.cloud"]);
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteUrl has_any (CampaignHosts) or tostring(parse_url(RemoteUrl).Host) in~ (CampaignHosts)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountUpn=InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, Indicator=coalesce(RemoteUrl, RemoteIP), Source="network", InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName;
let EvHits = DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType in ("DnsQueryResponse","ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionFailed","NetworkConnectionEvents")
  | where RemoteUrl has_any (CampaignHosts) or AdditionalFields has_any (CampaignHosts)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountUpn=InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, Indicator=coalesce(RemoteUrl, tostring(AdditionalFields)), Source="device-event", InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName=tostring(parse_json(""));
NetHits
| union EvHits
| order by Timestamp desc
let CampaignHosts = dynamic(["seed1.getsession.org","filev2.getsession.org","api.masscan.cloud"]);
let DnsHits = DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Name has_any (CampaignHosts)
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Indicator=Name, Source="DnsEvents";
let AsimDns = ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DnsQuery has_any (CampaignHosts)
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, Indicator=DnsQuery, Source="ImDnsActivity";
let ProxyHits = CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DestinationHostName has_any (CampaignHosts) or RequestURL has_any (CampaignHosts)
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer=SourceHostName, ClientIP=SourceIP, Indicator=coalesce(DestinationHostName, RequestURL), Source="Proxy/CEF";
let WebHits = ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where HttpHostName has_any (CampaignHosts) or Url has_any (CampaignHosts)
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, Indicator=coalesce(HttpHostName, Url), Source="ImWebSession";
DnsHits | union AsimDns, ProxyHits, WebHits
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count() by Computer, ClientIP, Indicator, Source
| order by LastSeen desc

TeamPCP Mini Shai-Hulud stealer payload hash match (SHA256/SHA1) AIInstallation High
Alerts on disk-write or in-memory execution of a binary whose SHA256 or SHA1 matches the obfuscated 2.3 MB credential-stealer payload published by TeamPCP across @tanstack, @uipath, @draftlab and other compromised npm packages. The hashes are the cleanest single-source-of-truth IOCs in this campaign and are reused unchanged across all 50+ compromised package versions. Rationale: Four SHA256 and three SHA1 hashes were published in the StepSecurity article as the canonical fingerprint of the 2.3 MB obfuscated stealer payload. These hashes were observed unchanged across all listed @tanstack/@uipath/@draftlab versions and were corroborated in earlier @antv variant reporting (Socket.dev, JFrog, StepSecurity — memory observations 1249, 1250, 1252). Hash-based hunting carries zero ambiguity and zero FP risk against benign software. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-a-self-spreading-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-npm-ecosystem • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized sandbox detonation by malware researchers on a forensic workstation
  • Internal threat-hunting team running yara/hash sweeps that touch the artifact during analysis
  • Backup or DLP product scanning a quarantined file and re-hashing it
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\SandboxAnalysis\\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("yara.exe","yara64.exe","capa.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Pivot on DeviceId to the InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm the parent is npm/node/bun/yarn, then enumerate which package and version installed (look in npm-cache or package-lock.json on the host). Step 2 (Contain): Isolate host, kill node/bun processes, force-rotate every credential reachable from that machine (npm tokens, GH PATs, cloud keys, AI tool keys, wallets, messaging app tokens), revoke any OIDC trust the host's CI runner role had. Step 3 (Hunt): Sweep org for the file hash on every host AND query DeviceFileEvents for any router_init.js drop in node_modules in the last 30d to find lateral worm spread.
let StealerSha256 = dynamic(["ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c","0c0e873033875f1bc471eda37e3b9d0f9b89bd41a4bbb4f86746caa2176c40aa","2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96","7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b"]);
let StealerSha1 = dynamic(["79ac49eedf774dd4b0cfa308722bc463cfe5885c","de0fac2e4500dabe0009e67214ff5f5447ce83dd","bbbca2ddaa5d8feaa63e36b76fdaad77386f024f"]);
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where SHA256 in~ (StealerSha256) or SHA1 in~ (StealerSha1) or InitiatingProcessSHA256 in~ (StealerSha256) or InitiatingProcessSHA1 in~ (StealerSha1)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, Source="DeviceProcessEvents";
let FileHits = DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where SHA256 in~ (StealerSha256) or SHA1 in~ (StealerSha1)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, Source="DeviceFileEvents";
let ImgHits = DeviceImageLoadEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where SHA256 in~ (StealerSha256) or SHA1 in~ (StealerSha1)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, Source="DeviceImageLoadEvents";
ProcHits | union FileHits, ImgHits
| order by Timestamp desc

let StealerSha1 = dynamic(["79ac49eedf774dd4b0cfa308722bc463cfe5885c","de0fac2e4500dabe0009e67214ff5f5447ce83dd","bbbca2ddaa5d8feaa63e36b76fdaad77386f024f"]);

Mini Shai-Hulud router_init.js dropped at npm package root in node_modules AIInstallation High
Detects file writes of a router_init.js file directly at a package root inside node_modules with a size > 1 MB on a single line — the exact filesystem signature documented in the StepSecurity comparison of clean (1.166.42) vs compromised (1.166.48) @tanstack tarballs (2,341,681 bytes, single line). Catches the worm at install time before the preinstall payload executes. Rationale: Table 2 in the article (Clean 1.166.42 vs Compromised 1.166.48) explicitly identifies router_init.js at root, 2,341,681 bytes, single line, as the structural marker of every compromised tarball. The file is absent from clean versions and is the worm's first-stage loader — file create from npm/node into node_modules is the exact moment of compromise. Cross-checked against the @antv variant analysis (memory observation 1247) which also noted the same loader file pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-a-self-spreading-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-npm-ecosystem • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1027 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate package coincidentally shipping a router_init.js at root (validate by hash — non-stealer hash + size != 2.3 MB single-line is FP)
  • Internal monorepo with a custom build step that generates router_init.js under node_modules cache
  • Developer extracting/inspecting the malicious tarball in a sandbox without executing
Suppression filter
| where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c","0c0e873033875f1bc471eda37e3b9d0f9b89bd41a4bbb4f86746caa2176c40aa","2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96","7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or FileSize between (2000000 .. 3500000)
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Capture SHA256 of the file and compare against the four known stealer hashes; check the package.json and package-lock.json in the parent directory to identify which compromised package landed on disk. Step 2 (Contain): Quarantine host, kill node processes, remove the node_modules tree, force-rotate any tokens stored in npm/git config on the host (npm tokens, GitHub PATs, ~/.aws/credentials, wallet seeds). Step 3 (Hunt): Search org for all npm publish events in last 30d from this user/runner identity AND for any GitHub commit authored as claude@users.noreply.github.com to find onward worm spread.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FileName =~ "router_init.js"
| where FolderPath has "node_modules"
| where FileSize > 1000000  // clean tarball baseline is no router_init.js; compromised version is ~2.3MB single line
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","npm","node","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","bun.exe","bun","corepack.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","bun.exe","corepack.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileCreate","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName =~ "router_init.js"
| where TargetFilePath has "node_modules"
| where TargetFileSize > 1000000
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm","pnpm","yarn","bun","corepack")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Mini Shai-Hulud router_init.js Drop in npm node_modules
id: a1c9d3e2-8a5d-4f1c-9d2e-1a8b3c5d7e09
description: Detects creation of router_init.js inside a node_modules tree by an npm/node/pnpm/yarn/bun process — TeamPCP's worm signature.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-a-self-spreading-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-npm-ecosystem
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/20
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1195.002
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_file:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '\router_init.js'
    TargetFilename|contains: '\node_modules\'
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\pnpm.exe'
      - '\yarn.exe'
      - '\bun.exe'
      - '\corepack.exe'
  condition: selection_file and selection_proc
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate npm package that ships a top-level router_init.js (verify by hash against the four known stealer SHA256s before suppressing)
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\node_modules\\*\\router_init.js OR *\\node_modules\\*\\Router_Init.js OR *\\node_modules\\*\\ROUTER_INIT.JS OR */node_modules/*/router_init.js) @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\npm.exe OR *\\pnpm.exe OR *\\yarn.exe OR *\\bun.exe OR */bin/node OR */bin/npm)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/[\\\/]node_modules[\\\/].*[\\\/]router_init\.js$/i
| WrittenBytes>1000000
| ContextImageFileName=/(node|npm|pnpm|yarn|bun|corepack)\.exe$/i OR ContextImageFileName=/\/(node|npm|pnpm|yarn|bun|corepack)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName, WrittenBytes], function=count())
| sort(_count, order=desc)
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="router_init.js" Filesystem.file_path="*node_modules*" (Filesystem.file_size>1000000 OR Filesystem.file_size="*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_hash Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
